Ablations further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does checking each finding against its cited evidence before it is reused. Because a model can answer correctly from memory alone, we also analyze the evidence retained by each harness. PANINI-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how harnesses compare and further strengthens PANINI-DR's advantage.
2610.15208.title: PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces

2610.15213.summary: We validate Leonid Space's space weather forecasts through comprehensive cross-validation of retroforecasts scored against the entire F10.7 and Ap historical record. We built a unified forecast model that jointly forecasts F10.7 and Ap on all timescales from 3 hours up to multi-decade chains of future solar cycles. This was used to generate an archive of historical 15-year retroforecasts, after performing a leave-one-out fit of the model on held-out data and conditioning only on historical data available at the time. The accuracy of this archive was scored against measured space weather indices at all lookahead horizons from 1 day to 15 years, using the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) as the primary quality metric. All other publicly available F10.7 and Ap forecast archives were scored using the same approach, including NASA's MSAFE and Schatten forecasts, SWPC's 27-day, 45-day, and Solar Cycle predictions, SWPC/USAF's RSGA, SIDC's Ursigram, CLS, Athens, KSO, BGS, SEPC's 3-day and 27-day forecasts, AFRL/NSO's SIFT, and BoM. Taken together, these 15 flux forecasts and 12 Ap forecasts compared on common lookahead metrics make up the most comprehensive cross-comparison of space weather forecasts we are aware of. Over a common forecast interval since 2000, Leonid had the lowest CRPS prediction error of any F10.7 or Ap prediction model: strictly lowest for Ap at all lookaheads and for F10.7 up to 5 years, and parity with MSAFE after 5 years. Much of this performance comes from our well-calibrated uncertainty bands, and we urge space weather forecasters to include calibrated uncertainties with their predictions and to issue retroforecast archives that can be used to rigorously evaluate their generating models.
2610.15213.title: Validation of Space Weather Forecasting at Leonid Space

2610.15280.summary: Depth estimation and Gaussian reconstruction share a need for multi-scale feature processing, yet use different prediction interfaces and training objectives. Whether a decoder's internal computation can be optimized once and reused across these systems remains a structural design question. Search over primitive configurations alone leaves the organization of transformations fixed. To address this gap, we propose GeoBridge, an evolutionary framework for transferable decoder topologies. First, GeoBridge makes stage-internal topology searchable through residual, sequential, and parallel composition of configurable primitives. Shape-preserving composition retains the stage interfaces of a fixed multi-scale scaffold. Second, a functional-tree encoding supports stage-aware crossover and hierarchical mutation, while a gradient sensitivity-alignment proxy evaluates candidates without training. Multi-objective evolution balances this proxy with computation and parameter cost. Third, selected topologies are instantiated and trained in target systems with task-specific prediction interfaces. A single source search takes approximately 12 GPU hours. GeoBridgeNet-A3 achieves the best depth accuracy among four adapted decoder baselines under a common encoder and training protocol on NYU Depth V2 and KITTI. The same topology reaches 27.11 dB PSNR in Gaussian novel-view synthesis on RealEstate10K, and its refined representations support open-vocabulary segmentation on LERF. These results support decoder topology as a reusable design object across the evaluated geometric vision systems. Code and pretrained weights are available at https://github.com/EMI-Group/GeoBridge-NAS.
2610.15280.title: GeoBridge: Evolving Transferable Decoder Topologies for Geometric Vision

2610.15307.summary: Efficient neural architecture search (NAS) requires accurate performance estimation under limited evaluation budgets. Existing zero-cost proxies (ZCPs) provide fast training-free signals, but each proxy usually captures only a partial property of an architecture, leading to unstable rankings across datasets and search spaces. In contrast, GNN-based predictors can improve accuracy, but often depend on labeled architectures, graph encoders, and costly representation learning, which makes them less suitable for extreme few-shot settings. We propose FENAS, a topology-agnostic few-shot prediction framework that turns complementary initialization priors into robust ranking signals. Its core component, CAST, is a feature pipeline that combines copula alignment and synergy transformation. CAST maps heterogeneous ZCPs into a compact feature manifold, enabling lightweight meta-learners to produce reliable rankings from scarce supervision. On NAS-Bench-201, with only 0.5% labeled samples, FENAS achieves a Kendall's Tau ($τ$) of 0.70, outperforming representative topology-based few-shot predictors in this low-label regime. In closed-domain search, FENAS evaluates the NAS-Bench-201 space in approximately 1138 seconds and achieves competitive test accuracy. By providing a fast, reliable, and structurally simple evaluation mechanism, FENAS supports the design of automated neural architectures under limited evaluation budgets.
2610.15307.title: FENAS: A Few-Shot Meta-Ensembling Framework for Efficient Neural Architecture Search with Synergized Zero-Cost Proxies

2610.15345.summary: High-quality coding problems are expensive to collect. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench rely on substantial human curation, while synthetic alternatives typically rely on costly model generation and validation. In this work, we show that new coding problems can be created at almost no cost by composing existing ones. We formulate problem generation as code composition: verified atomic problems are combined into level-$N$ tasks, and a task is kept only if every atomic problem remains unsolved and a joint reference solution passes the same check used at evaluation time. The entire task-construction process is programmatic and requires no language-model generation or validation. We instantiate this approach in four coding settings: multi-bug repair, proof completion, complexity analysis, and clone equivalence. The generated tasks are challenging for frontier models, which all degrade as compositional depth increases. The generated tasks are also useful as training data: rejection-sampling fine-tuning on them improves Qwen3.5-9B at every composition level.
2610.15345.title: CodeWalk: Generating Coding Benchmarks by Walking a Problem Graph

2610.15355.summary: Multi-frequency electrical impedance tomography (EIT) often requires specialized hardware. This challenge is especially pronounced in biomedical applications. We developed a 16-electrode EIT system using an Arduino GIGA R1 WiFi for generation and acquisition, with a discrete current source, three analog multiplexers, and basic signal conditioning. Dual cores separate waveform timing from switching and acquisition. A 3D-printed tank with silver-wire electrodes was tested at 11 frequencies (1-180 kHz). Across the 10-180 kHz analysis band, median repeat-frame signal-to-noise ratio was 48 dB, acquisition rate was ~0.18 frames/s per frequency (~60 s per sweep), and cross-session baseline drift was ~6%. KCl phantoms contained an insulating ABS cylinder or KCl-filled dialysis bags (0.001-1.0 M) spanning positive and negative conductivity contrasts. Boundary voltages were analyzed without reconstruction to estimate inclusion position, contrast polarity, and relative magnitude. Leave-one-session-out matching located ABS inclusions in 29/30 runs at 160 kHz (87-97% across the band; chance 33%). For dialysis bags, polarity was correctly identified in all 36 nonzero-contrast runs. Signed voltage projections correlated with the cylindrical contrast factor (R^2=0.68 across runs; R^2=0.89 for the aggregate fit). Concentration was ordered (Spearman rho=0.85), despite saturation above ~10-fold contrast. Bag position accuracy ranged from 6/6 at the highest contrasts to 2/6 at matched conductivity. The matched-conductivity bag produced a ~1.7% RMS perturbation against 0.4-0.6% repeat-frame variability. These results demonstrate that microcontroller-based multi-frequency EIT can support selected detection and identification tasks through direct boundary-voltage analysis, supporting future studies of muscle electrochemistry.
2610.15355.title: An Arduino Giga-Based Multi-Frequency Electrical Impedance Tomography System for Electrolyte Media: Hardware Design, Statistical Voltage Analysis, and System Performance Evaluation

2610.15388.summary: Contrastive representation learning (CRL) is a fundamental paradigm for learning transferable representations. Recent work identifies its population target as the pointwise mutual information (PMI) $\log\frac{p(x,y)}{p_X(x)p_Y(y)}$ between two modalities $X,Y$, where $p$ is the joint density function and $p_X,p_Y$ are the marginals. However, it remains unclear why standard inner-product scores $f(x)^\top g(y)$ can effectively approximate a generally nonseparable population target PMI. In this paper, we address this question from the aspect of approximation for CRL. By linking PMI to a compact operator, we show that $D$-dimensional inner-product models perform rank-$D$ spectral approximation, with error controlled by the spectral tail. We then study neural network realizations: in general settings, we show that deep neural network scoring functions are universally consistent, and the approximation error rates depend on the smoothness of the PMI function; under structured low-rank data models we obtain improved rates attained by moderate-width encoders. Finally, we establish a fast calibration rate from contrastive excess risk to downstream retrieval error under a density-ratio Tsybakov noise condition.
2610.15388.title: Approximation in Contrastive Representation Learning

2610.15658.summary: Distributed Constraint Satisfaction Problems (DCSPs) model distributed decision-making in multi-agent systems, where agents assign values to local variables while satisfying shared constraints. However, many DCSP solvers still rely on broad, repeated peer-to-peer communication and are largely reactive, with limited support for strategic coordination or learning. This increases communication overhead, can lead to stagnation, and reduces the success of hard instances. Hence, we propose Dynamic Conflict Clustering-Incomplete (DCC-Incomplete), a repair-based solver that combines conflict-centred decomposition, structured coordination, strategic repair, and lightweight learning for stagnation recovery. DCC-Incomplete groups the unsolved part of the problem into conflict clusters and restricts communication via a coordination layer to agents within the same conflict region. It also introduces memory-guided restart, enabling agents and clusters to pause, revise, and adapt repairs based on neighbouring conflict states. A thorough evaluation of DCC-Incomplete on distributed graph-colouring benchmarks with planted satisfying assignments shows that its memory-guided restart improves the success rate from 37.50% to 61.11%, reduces median runtime from 0.565s to 0.367s, and cuts median communication from 12.493 to 6.503 messages per constraint. These results suggest that dynamic conflict clustering, combined with lightweight strategic and learning-guided repair, improves both communication efficiency and robustness in incomplete DCSP solving.
2610.15658.title: Dynamic Conflict Clustering with Lightweight Learning and Strategic Repair for Distributed Constraint Satisfaction

2610.15685.summary: Conventional distillation transfers capability through teacher-generated demonstrations. LLM-as-a-Judge knowledge distillation offers a distinct and increasingly practical alternative. In the label-only variant studied here, the student generates every response and improves from scalar scores alone. Prior work shows that this non-demonstrative feedback can improve student capability, but it creates a fundamentally different provenance problem. No teacher-generated answer enters the student's training set, so any evaluator-specific trace must pass through a low-bandwidth reward signal rather than copied text. Existing watermarks and distillation detectors do not cover this score-only channel. We introduce Radioactive Feedback, which encodes a registered pattern of behavioral preferences in the rewards themselves. The evaluator applies bounded pointwise adjustments to quality-qualified responses, allowing repeated optimization to transfer the pattern to a student trained by another party. Experiments on code and mathematics show that the registered preferences transfer through scores alone and across datasets, enabling black-box detection against a fixed reference pool.
2610.15685.title: Radioactive Feedback: Tracing Models Trained by Label-Only LLM Supervision

2610.15791.summary: Ordinal optimization selects designs that are good enough rather than optimal when evaluation is expensive and the budget is small. The alignment probability measures the chance that the selected set contains at least a prescribed number of truly good designs. We formulate quantum ordinal optimization as a class of problems that maximize this probability under a fixed oracle budget. We study exact, coherent pairwise comparisons with one selected design as a first instance, with the budget counted in comparison queries. For every classical comparison budget smaller than the number of designs, we prove that a knockout among uniformly sampled designs attains the optimum. The sample is drawn without replacement and contains one more design than the number of comparisons. For a uniformly random order, the selected design's rank has a polynomial probability law. At the same comparison budget, the maximum quantum degree is at most twice the classical maximum, a factor attained whenever there are more than twice as many designs as comparisons, so a quantum algorithm can realize rank laws that no classical algorithm with the same budget can. We determine the exact quantum optimum with one comparison for every number of designs and every good-enough set. For selecting the best of n designs, the optimal success probability with one quantum comparison is approximately 3.30/n for large n, compared with 2/n for one classical comparison. When the best design is sought, one quantum comparison gives a higher alignment probability than two classical comparisons whenever there are more than nine designs.
2610.15791.title: Quantum ordinal optimization under a fixed comparison budget

2610.15896.summary: In sequential learning, a group of agents sequentially receives a noisy private signal and observes the predictions of prior agents to estimate a hidden ground truth. While extensively studied for binary signals, we formalize and analyze sequential learning when the hidden ground truth is an ordering of $n$ items, and both private signals and inferences involve pairwise comparisons. A key focus in sequential learning is herding, where agents disregard their private signals to follow the crowd. We show that, while local herding in our model may lead agents to make incorrect pairwise inferences, the global hidden order can still be approximated. Specifically, by aggregating all pairwise comparison outputs, the highest-ranked items can be retrieved. We investigate top-$k$ retrieval across three scenarios: (1) passive aggregation, where information is gathered from the social learning process without intervention; (2) strategic selection, where agents choose their pairwise comparisons dynamically; and (3) aggregation with stubborn nodes, where a very small set of stubborn agents, who base their inferences solely on their private signals, join the mechanism. With query complexity as the number of agents needed for a high-probability estimation, we propose top-$k$ retrieval algorithms with query complexities sublinear in $O(n^2)$, the total number of pairs.
2610.15896.title: Social Learning of Ranking: Getting the Top Right despite Local Herding

2610.15924.summary: Agent environments are essential for large language model (LLM) development. They use programmatic verifiers to turn complex outcomes into rewards. Verifiers can be attacked into awarding full credit to cheating agents without completing the intended task, causing inaccurate evaluation and misalignment in training. As agent environments scale in numbers and difficulty, so must the repairing of exploitable verifiers. To this end, we ask whether today's model with scaled compute can automatically harden agent environments to prevent potentially stronger future models from reward hacking. We introduce a scalable, fully automatic approach to weak-to-strong verifier hardening. It first sets up an isolated verifier sandbox that agents cannot directly modify, then uses a hacker-fixer loop to find and repair remaining verifier vulnerabilities. We apply this loop to Terminal Bench, KernelBench, and SETA, substantially reducing attack success across these agent environments. The iterative design scales with the hardening budget, producing progressively stronger defenses as the number of loop iterations increases and outperforming the static, non-iterative baseline. An earlier version of our hacker-fixer loop has been adopted by the official Terminal Bench repository as a way to audit exploits in its environments. Project page: https://verifier-hardening.github.io/.
2610.15924.title: Scalable Weak-to-Strong Verifier Hardening for Agent Environments

2610.15932.summary: Computing equilibria in high-dimensional continuous games requires learning and representing rich, multi-modal strategy distributions, something conventional neural policies struggle to achieve. Diffusion models offer a natural solution, but standard diffusion training requires direct samples from a fixed target distribution, which are generally unavailable under iterative game-solving updates. We propose a diffusion-based framework for equilibrium computation that enables diffusion-based variants of Online Mirror Descent (OMD) and Fictitious Play (FP). Our approach derives a reweighted score-matching objective that trains diffusion policies without requiring direct samples from each updated policy. Our main method, DiffNash, combines the fast convergence of OMD with the sample efficiency of FP by reusing past actions through a replay buffer. To correct the resulting distribution shift from sample reuse, we derive an unbiased estimator of the difference between current and past policies' Evidence Lower Bounds, whose exponential provides a tractable proxy for the corresponding importance weight without evaluating diffusion likelihoods. We evaluate our approach on forest protection games and continuous Colonel Blotto games, reducing the Nash gap over the strongest baseline by 35.6% and 24.7%, respectively, with minimal hyperparameter tuning.
2610.15932.title: DiffNash: Finding Nash Equilibrium in High-Dimensional Continuous Action Spaces with Diffusion Policies

2610.15938.summary: Evaluation of text generated by large language models (LLMs) is increasingly delegated to LLMs acting as judges, yet what such a judge must be shown remains unresolved. We treat a judge whose reports are acted on as a regulator, in the sense of cybernetics, and ask what it must be shown, how much, in what form, and what its reports must get right. On seven public benchmarks we varied only what the judge was shown. Across three judges whose prices differ 10- to 17-fold, what the judge was shown mattered more than which judge it was. When a system revised its answers on feedback from a judge denied the material they had to respect, it ended below its starting point on instruction following and question answering. On instruction following the loss grew with each round, and it persisted when the judge saw the user's request but not the constraints and with a second judge family. On news summarisation, a correct reference summary beside the source undid most of the source's contribution, whereas on single-answer questions a reference helped. About a tenth of the source did almost all of its work, and a small entailment graph matched an LLM judge at finding errors in grounded text. We committed 83 testable clauses before running; of the 81 that ran, 32 met their bar and 50 went in the predicted direction, and most quantitative predictions from the theory failed. We report every shortfall and derive design rules tied to measured effects.
2610.15938.title: The Anatomy of a Blind Spot: What an LLM Judge Must Be Shown, and How Much

2610.15950.summary: We study particle approximations of maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) flows with the Coulomb kernel on the torus $\mathbb{T}^d$, $d\ge2$, driven by thermal noise of strength $τ\ge0$. For smooth, strictly positive initial and target densities and i.i.d. initial positions, we prove that the expected Wasserstein-1 distance between the empirical measure and the mean-field solution is at most of order $N^{-1/d}$ for $d\ge3$ and $\sqrt{(\log N)/N}$ for $d=2$, uniformly in time and in the temperature $τ\ge0$, including the deterministic case $τ=0$. At each fixed $τ>0$, we also prove propagation of chaos in total variation for any $k$-fold marginal distributions of particles, uniformly in time, with a bound of order $\sqrt{k/τ}$ times the empirical convergence rate. Our proof uses the modulated free-energy method of Bresch, Jabin, and Wang to reduce the particle convergence estimate to a relaxation estimate that controls the time integral of the mean-field velocity gradient uniformly in $τ\ge0$. Near zero temperature, where the smoothing effect of the noise degenerates, we obtain this estimate by recentering the dynamics at thermal equilibrium and using the damping generated by the Coulomb interaction.
2610.15950.title: Uniform-in-Time and Uniform-in-Temperature Particle Approximations of Coulomb MMD Flows

2610.15958.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated across ophthalmic tasks, yet the methodological quality of these evaluations has received little attention. Most studies report accuracy while overlooking design features required for valid and clinically meaningful inference. We critically reviewed published ophthalmic LLM evaluation studies covering knowledge assessment, patient education, diagnostic reasoning, triage, clinical documentation, multimodal image interpretation, and uncertainty estimation. We used the methodological weaknesses that recurred across study designs to develop the SIGHT framework, which has five domains: Sample and item provenance, Independence and blinding, Ground truth and comparator fairness, Handling of paired and repeated-measures data, and Transparency and trustworthiness. Current evaluations rely heavily on benchmark accuracy, synthetic clinical vignettes, and curated datasets, and real-world clinical validation remains rare. Common limitations include potential training-data contamination, inadequate handling of paired data, limited assessment of inter-rater reliability, inconsistent reference standards, insufficient evaluation of calibration and uncertainty, and frequent overinterpretation of benchmark performance as evidence of clinical readiness. SIGHT provides twenty structured appraisal items to evaluate internal validity, interpretability, and applicability across diverse ophthalmic LLM study designs. It offers a practical way to appraise ophthalmic LLM studies and may improve the methodological quality, interpretability, and clinical relevance of future evaluations.
2610.15958.title: SIGHT: A Methodological Appraisal Framework for Evaluating Large Language Models in Ophthalmology

2610.15988.summary: Authorization checks at individual tool calls do not reveal how long earlier authority remains usable. We study this lifecycle failure as privilege creep: a capability stays reachable after its last justified workflow step. We present CreepScope, a trace-oriented evaluation protocol that samples reachable authority at every step and separates no-remaining-use exposure into stale-after-use and never-required components; Capability-Step Exposure (CSE) counts total stepwise overexposure and Residual Privilege Debt (RPD) the terminal residue, while stale-after-use exposure is the direct privilege-creep measure. A 96-cell deterministic replay over 12 controlled storage, communication, and cloud-operation workflows validates these semantics: Static Task Scope and Monotonic On-Demand retain mean CSEs of 26 and 13, whereas an oracle-controlled Step Lease has zero CSE and zero residual debt by construction. All three persistent regimes share the same stale-after-use exposure of 13, so their CSE differences come from scope and grant timing rather than post-use retention; Full Access alone adds 91.33 never-required capability-steps. A separate 24-episode local case then lets Qwen2 7B choose tools in one simulated mail workflow: the injected stale send executes in all nine persistent-policy episodes and in none of the three Step-Lease episodes, while all 24 required action sequences complete. These results establish a reproducible containment case, not cross-workflow or cross-model effectiveness. Core metrics are reconstructed from raw events, and exact gates reject incomplete or duplicated evaluation grids.
2610.15988.title: CreepScope: Measuring Post-Use Authorization Exposure in Tool-Using Agents

2610.16057.summary: Current-generation 21-cm surveys of extragalactic neutral hydrogen (HI) with instruments such as FAST and ASKAP are providing detailed spectral and spatial information for over 10^5 galaxies. Future HI surveys with next-generation radio telescopes could provide sample sizes larger by orders of magnitude. There is therefore a need for accurate, automated, and reliable parameterisation of the HI emission from galaxies. We have developed an automated estimator for HI global profile widths to better enable studies of, for example, dynamical masses and Tully-Fisher distances. Our estimator is based on an implementation of the BusyFit profile-fitting algorithm, and converges for 95% of global profiles in the WALLABY pilot survey. Probability density functions are calculated for all profile parameters using Monte Carlo techniques, and example error parameterisations are given. We confirm that linewidth uncertainties depend primarily on the integrated signal-to-noise ratio, profile steepness, and the linewidth, consistent with previous studies. We compare several common linewidth definitions, and the width at 50% of the mean flux density (Wm50) is found to be the most robust measure of linewidth. We provide examples of the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation drawn from the WALLABY pilot survey.
2610.16057.title: WALLABY pilot survey: accurate and automated linewidth measurements from global HI profiles

2610.16067.summary: Agent evaluation harnesses are software systems that run test suites, generate inputs, and decide outcomes with test oracles. This paper audits such software for reliability defects that score tables cannot reveal. We introduce an oracle-integrity auditing approach with five state-integrity invariants and three known-answer controls. We evaluate it by injecting seven oracle defect classes across two task domains and a synthetic domain. All injected defect classes are detected, and the repaired oracle has no false positives. Applied to an agent benchmark, the audit reveals a reward-function defect that changes the environment state before post-run scoring. Across 4,320 episodes, replay-based correction changes database-pass labels from 4,194 to 2,883 and reduces measured success from 94.3% to 65.5%. We also study configuration-dependent measurement effects. A component ablation over 3,240 episodes shows that the agent's policy documents, tool descriptions, and tool error strings influence observed trajectory reliability, with tool descriptions showing the largest exploratory effect (-9.2 pp) and error strings the smallest (-5.3 pp). A second task domain reverses the sign of the language effect, so the result is bounded to the tested configuration. Finally, we report a portability boundary: the auditing approach cannot validate a second independently implemented benchmark because the required reference terminal state cannot be reconstructed from its recorded API-call log. The paper releases a replication package containing the auditing suite, fault-injection catalogue, frozen records, deviation logs, and offline analysis entry points without network access, API keys, or model calls.
2610.16067.title: When Agent Evaluation Becomes Unreliable: An Empirical Study of Oracle Failures and Configuration-Dependent Measurement in an LLM Agent Benchmark

2610.16071.summary: Reliable deployment of LLM-based multi-agent systems calls for runtime auditors that predict terminal outcomes from observed execution prefixes. These auditors typically learn from a limited corpus of trajectories with verified outcomes. Expanding this corpus requires costly execution and verification, yet broader failure coverage alone provides no explicit criterion for identifying prefixes that the current auditor finds difficult to classify. To this end, we propose Dream2Discern, a runtime auditor trained through implicit augmentation guided by its own prediction loss. During Dream, we select perturbations of the auditor's representation operators to increase prediction loss on recorded prefixes, yielding hard latent variants. During Discern, the auditor learns to predict execution outcomes from these variants using the original labels. The variants are regenerated as the auditor learns, turning a limited corpus into a renewable source of hard examples and requiring no additional trajectory collection or outcome verification. Extensive evaluations on AFTraj-2K and StepShield show that Dream2Discern outperforms competitive failure auditors and achieves over 90% trajectory-level weighted accuracy on both benchmarks while balancing prediction accuracy and timeliness. Project page: https://zbox1005.github.io/dream2discern-project/
2610.16071.title: Dream2Discern: Learning from Hard Latent Variants for Runtime Failure Prediction in Multi-Agent Systems

2610.16117.summary: LLM-based multi-agent collaboration is increasingly used to solve complex tasks by dividing work among specialized agents and integrating complementary expertise. Yet existing systems and evaluations largely rest on an implicit perfect-colleague assumption: collaborators provide correct and complete information and respond promptly to requests. In realistic teamwork, however, collaborators may return information that does not answer the intended question, provide insufficient detail to support a decision, or fail to respond to a request. To separate task-solving competence from the ability to recover an unreliable evidence-gathering process, we introduce the Unreliable Colleagues Benchmark (UnCoBench), which organizes behavioral failures through Misaligned, Incomplete, and Missed settings. The main agent need to verify contextual correctness, diagnose information gap and track unresolved dependencies in order to obtain the correct evidence for solving the task. We also introduce a verifiable and scalable automated generation pipeline that pairs LLM-based scenario generation with executable checks of answer uniqueness and role necessity. Results across ten models show that similar reliable-setting performance can result in different robustness to unreliable evidence. Trace analysis reveals frequent omissions of corrective follow-up, and the recovery behavior involves inefficient waiting and redundant queries. These findings show that robust collaboration requires not only sound reasoning, but also targeted action to diagnose evidence failures, recover relevant information, and integrate it into decisions. Our data and source code are available at https://github.com/iNLP-Lab/UnCoBench.
2610.16117.title: Beyond Perfect Teammates: Multi-Agent Collaboration with Unreliable Colleagues

2610.16152.summary: Although post-training significantly enhances model performance, the use of massive undisclosed data raises concerns about benchmark contamination and copyright infringement. This drives growing interest in training data detection for post-trained models. Existing evaluations for training data detection often leverage benchmarks constructed post hoc, which can introduce distribution shifts. Alternatively, controlled evaluations rely on small-scale training setups that diverge from realistic post-training settings. As a result, their reported performance may not faithfully reflect the effectiveness of detection methods in real-world scenarios. To this end, we introduce \textsc{\method}, a reliable benchmark designed to evaluate detection methods in realistic, large-scale post-training settings. Built on a multi-stage pipeline, \method\space encompasses stage-specific models throughout the post-training lifecycle, spanning SFT, DPO, and RL. To perform a reliable evaluation, we construct model-specific evaluation sets across four diverse tasks, featuring distribution-matched members and non-members with verifiable membership labels. Our results reveal that even the best-performing method achieves an average AUC of only 0.529 on our benchmark, which approaches random-guessing level (0.5). Furthermore, our analysis suggests that evaluation protocols can significantly affect measured detection performance. These findings highlight the significant potential for developing effective, practical, and robust detection methods under realistic scenarios.
2610.16152.title: WildTrace: Evaluating Training Data Detection in Realistic Large-Scale LLM Post-Training

2610.16187.summary: Existing cumulative regret guarantees for Bayesian optimization (BO) do not necessarily characterize the quality of the algorithm's final output. This gap is critical under noisy evaluations, where the goal is to return a single high-quality recommendation. To address it, we introduce efficient exploration strategies that can be incorporated into any BO procedure by occasionally replacing the acquisition query with an exploration query. To validate this approach, we bound the Gaussian process posterior standard deviation over the search space via the fill distance of the queries, which measures the largest region left unexplored. We then use this result to derive upper bounds on the inference regret, i.e., the gap between the global optimum and the function value at the algorithm's returned point. Empirically, these exploration strategies improve the final recommendations of existing BO algorithms on synthetic benchmarks, hyperparameter optimization, and a control task.
2610.16187.title: Exploration strategies for Gaussian process bandit optimization with inference regret guarantees

2610.16236.summary: Morphogenesis is driven by the interplay of genetic regulation and tissue mechanics. In vivo video data is limited, particularly under genetic mutations and environmental perturbations, making generalization beyond the most representative conditions in the dataset challenging. However, at tissue scales, the dynamics of Drosophila can be described as a continuum flow, motivating the usage of representations learned across other physical systems as priors for developmental dynamics. We investigate finetuning Walrus, a Continuum Dynamics Foundation Model pretrained across a broad set of simulated continuous systems, on tissue velocity fields from only 12 wild-type Drosophila blastoderm videos. We evaluate autoregressive prediction both in-distribution and zero-shot under unseen temperature and genetic perturbations. Zero-shot refers to evaluation on perturbation conditions never seen during wild-type finetuning, without any additional training. In-distribution, a Fourier Neural Operator model trained from scratch achieves best performance on VRMSE. However, Walrus (CRPS) is the strongest model under the most severe distribution shift of unseen samples of mutated embryos and temperature conditions. Interestingly, predictions capture the shape of the mean surface tissue velocity trajectory and its separation between 17°C and 27°C, including the timing of the peak at Germ Band Extension onset, a biologically meaningful milestone of embryo development. Our results provide preliminary support that representations learned from different dynamical systems can transfer to experimental morphogenesis in developmental regimes, provided they admit a continuum description. More broadly, our results motivate further study of physics foundation models as a new complementary tool for the simulation of morphogenesis in low-data regimes.
2610.16236.title: From Simulated Fluids to Living Tissue: Zero-Shot Foundation Model Transfer to Perturbed Embryos

2610.16319.summary: Real-world hybrid web tasks need both information gathering and page interaction, yet search-based and operation-based agents are developed and evaluated separately. To bridge this gap, we introduce HyWe, a framework that unifies both capabilities within one model and trajectory. Its two modes use dedicated prompts and tool sets to sustain sub-goal execution; explicit switching selects the needed capability, and shared history lets each mode build on the other's findings. To provide demonstrations of these behaviors, we develop HyWeCollector, a fully automatic pipeline that uses task prototypes, four switching patterns, and multi-agent synthesis to produce verified hybrid trajectories. We train HyWe-35B on these demonstrations to unify efficient information gathering and browser interaction in a single 35B web agent. To evaluate hybrid task completion, we introduce HyWeBench: 100 human-written tasks on websites distinct from training, with human-written sub-goal checklists and an outcome-based evaluation pipeline. Hybrid training enables HyWe-35B to achieve 47.0% success on this benchmark, improving on the untrained base model by 19.0 percentage points and outperforming existing search-based and operation-based agents. Even before training, the same base model solves 28.0% of tasks with HyWe, versus 11.0% with all tools under one prompt. Beyond hybrid tasks, HyWe-35B achieves 59.0% and 88.3% success on Online-Mind2Web and WebVoyager, outperforming existing open-source baselines and cutting action cost per successful task by 48.3% and 51.9% compared with Fara-7B.
2610.16319.title: HyWe: Unifying Search and Operation for Real-World Hybrid Web Tasks

2610.16329.summary: Accurate breast cancer risk prediction from screening mammography is essential for improved risk stratification and personalized screening. It can benefit from both temporal breast tissue changes across longitudinal examinations and complementary anatomical information from craniocaudal (CC) and mediolateral oblique (MLO) views. Leveraging longitudinal information requires identifying corresponding tissue regions across examinations, yet most approaches rely on implicit feature alignment without explicitly enforcing spatial consistency. Recent work has demonstrated the benefits of explicit temporal alignment; however, existing methods model each view independently, preventing them from exploiting complementary CC and MLO information. Furthermore, explicit approaches have been limited to a single prior examination. To fill these gaps, we propose (github.com/sot176/FlexLMV-Net), a breast-wise longitudinal multi-view framework that jointly models CC and MLO views across screening examinations while accommodating a variable number of prior examinations. FlexLMV-Net explicitly aligns longitudinal feature maps and integrates complementary views through cross-view temporal fusion and a dual-stream attention block. Evaluated on EMBED and CSAW-CC, FlexLMV-Net consistently outperforms existing approaches across breast density, cancer subtypes, and demographic subgroups, highlighting the benefits of explicit longitudinal alignment, multi-view modeling, and flexible use of available screening history. We further introduce (github.com/sot176/BCRBench), an open-source benchmark that unifies state-of-the-art single- and multi-timepoint breast cancer risk prediction models under standardized preprocessing, training, inference, and evaluation protocols, enabling fair and reproducible comparison of existing methods.
2610.16329.title: Explicitly Aligned Multi-View Breast Cancer Risk Prediction from Variable-Length Screening Histories

2610.16423.summary: Sprite-based animation remains prevalent in video game development, but manual in-betweening---generating intermediate frames between keyframes---is labor-intensive. Existing video frame interpolation methods, optimized for photorealistic content, introduce smoothing artifacts when applied to the sharp edges, limited color palettes, and stylized motion characteristic of hand-drawn sprites. We present a deep learning approach for sprite in-betweening that adapts a U-Net encoder-decoder architecture with domain-specific modifications, including RGBA-aware processing, multi-scale flow refinement, and alpha-gated blending to preserve pixel-perfect sprite aesthetics. Following data-centric AI principles, we demonstrate that a few carefully curated sprite animation triplets---selected for diversity, quality, and representative edge cases---enable effective training without requiring massive generic datasets. Experimental evaluation using the FLIP perceptual metric shows that our method achieves a mean error of 0.258 on 42 test triplets, outperforming state-of-the-art video interpolation RIFE (0.313, 17.5\% worse), traditional optical flow Lucas-Kanade (0.449, 42.6\% worse), and general frame synthesis CyclicGen (0.603, 57.2\% worse). This study shows that quality-over-quantity data curation and domain-specific architectural adaptations yield better interpolation quality than general-purpose methods trained on orders of magnitude more data, validating the data-centric AI paradigm for specialized visual domains. This is particularly important for small-to-medium-sized game development studios, where budget and time constraints are critical.
2610.16423.title: Low-Cost Deep Learning for Automated Keyframe Interpolation in Sprite Animation

2610.16450.summary: The growing use of language models for forecasting motivates a broader evaluation of their world-model capabilities. Such evaluation must go beyond predictive accuracy to assess hidden-state inference and intervention prediction. Real-world forecasting benchmarks offer limited access to hidden-state ground truth and controlled experiments. We introduce CivWorldBench, a benchmark built on a multi-agent strategy game engine with recorded internal states, controlled observations, and paired intervention rollouts. Its 1,900 decision points from 475 worlds support three task levels: association forecasting, belief inference, and intervention prediction. Reference predictors support attributable evaluation of capability gaps, with an expert harness and empirical ceiling estimates contextualizing scores. Stored trajectories make intermediate predictions verifiable, while agent-play experiments test whether world-model capabilities support decision-making. The main panel comprises eleven frontier language models. Composite benchmark scores correlate with real-world forecasting leaderboards on matched model panels, more closely than with a general-capability index, supporting its use as a proxy for real-world forecasting capability. Strong association forecasts do not consistently extend to belief inference or intervention prediction, and effect magnitudes remain poorly calibrated despite informative direction predictions. Process verification reveals errors missed by final-answer evaluation, and structured reasoning improves intervention prediction for the strongest model in the process study. Agent-play experiments identify useful assisted plans and motivate evaluating decision-relevant capabilities beyond association forecasting. These findings identify hidden-state inference, intermediate-state prediction, and effect calibration as priorities for world-model training.
2610.16450.title: CivWorldBench: Evaluating Language World Models in Structured Multi-Agent Sandbox Worlds

2610.16538.summary: We present PatTransBench, a 12,000-item Chinese-English/Japanese/Korean patent machine translation (PatMT) benchmark with a four-dimensional evaluation protocol. The benchmark comprises 6,000 short-text (sentence/claim) and 6,000 long-text (paragraph) pairs, evenly split across three language pairs and both translation directions, built via IPC-section-stratified sampling and dualthreshold quality gating from upstream patent-family parallel corpora. The evaluation protocol spans literal n-gram overlap (BLEU, ROUGE-L, chrF), cross-lingual semantic textual similarity (CLSTS), 38-probe-language consistency testing, and serving performance under concurrency. A case study on PatMT2-7B and its fp8/AWQ4/AutoRound-4bit variants reveals direction-dependent quantization effects masked by aggregate scores and non-monotonic language-failure patterns across quantization schemes that are invisible to single-metric evaluation. We plan to release the benchmark, protocol, and case-study results upon publication to support reproducible PatMT evaluation.
2610.16538.title: PatTransBench: an ipc-stratified, multi-dimensional benchmark for patent machine translation evaluation

2610.16567.summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have achieved high success rates on familiar manipulation tasks, yet it remains unclear whether such scores reflect genuine zero-shot generalization and perturbation robustness. Existing evaluation frameworks provide limited capability-level diagnosis and combinatorial perturbation coverage, often without connecting diagnosis to targeted model refinement. We introduce VLA-GAUGE, a diagnostic framework that unifies both evaluations under a shared executable task representation. It combines (1) paired in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks across six capability suites, (2) single-factor sensitivity analysis with combinatorial perturbation screening and evaluation, and (3) diagnosis-driven refinement through targeted data augmentation and model fine-tuning. We evaluate 12 VLAs spanning different model sizes and action-modeling paradigms under a unified protocol. We find that (1) The mean Zero-Shot Score on VLA-GAUGE is only 22.3%, with SimpleVLA-RL scoring 8.0% and ranking second to last among the evaluated models. (2) Under three representative combinatorial perturbation configurations, the mean R-Score is 9.3. (3) Diagnosis-driven fine-tuning improves $π_{0.5}$'s zero-shot generalization and robustness under a selected perturbation combination on held-out scenarios by 72.4 and 31.8 scoring points, respectively; the latter exceeds the 10.9-point gain from LIBERO-Plus single-factor fine-tuning despite fewer successful training trajectories. These results show that high reported success rates on familiar manipulation tasks do not guarantee strong zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks or robustness to combinatorial perturbations, while diagnostic evaluation provides actionable signals for targeted model improvement.
2610.16567.title: VLA-GAUGE: Systematically Evaluating Generalization and Robustness in Vision-Language-Action Models

2610.16569.summary: Relevance prediction between user queries and items is a fundamental component of e-commerce search systems. Traditionally, high-quality relevance labels are obtained through human judgment, which is reliable but expensive, slow, and difficult to scale. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) enable automated relevance judgment at scale, achieving performance comparable to human annotators. However, such systems often rely on large commercial LLMs with complex prompts, resulting in high inference costs and limited throughput. In this work, we propose a framework that bridges this gap by distilling a high-performing LLM-based relevance judgment system into efficient multimodal student models. We first curate a small, high-quality human-annotated dataset to serve as ground truth. Using this dataset, we develop a reliable LLM-as-a-judge pipeline through careful prompt engineering and iterative refinement. This pipeline is then used to generate large-scale relevance labels, which serve as training data for compact multimodal models. Our distilled models achieve performance close to the teacher system while significantly improving latency, cost, and scalability. This approach enables practical deployment of high-quality relevance prediction systems in production environments.
2610.16569.title: From a Large-Scale Teacher to Efficient Multimodal Students for Search Relevance Prediction

2610.16634.summary: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models increasingly use natural-language instructions to condition autonomous driving behavior. Yet existing closed-loop benchmarks primarily measure route completion, safety, and rule compliance, leaving a fundamental question unresolved: does language actually determine which feasible behavior the vehicle executes? A trajectory may be safe and successful while still violating or even ignoring the passenger's instruction. To address this, we introduce \ltd, a benchmark designed to directly test this capability. Its key evaluation unit, the paired counterfactual unit (PCU), holds the initial driving scene fixed while changing only the instruction. This design enables us to distinguish isolated instruction success from counterfactual paired success across four instruction-following scopes. To test whether this distinction persists across evaluation regimes, we instantiate Language2Drive in complementary closed-loop CARLA simulation, reconstructed real-world scenes, and open-loop driving benchmarks, including our released CARLA-Language2Drive simulator with purpose-built maps. Evaluating representative driving VLAs across these settings reveals a striking mismatch between strong driving competence and weak language control: 93.2% of successful rollouts do not have a successful counterpart under the alternative feasible instruction. This failure is dominated by one-sided completion, where a model repeatedly executes one preferred behavior but fails when the same scene requires the counterfactual alternative. These results expose two fundamental limitations of current evaluation: isolated success and driving scores, which are widely used by conventional driving benchmarks, can substantially overstate language-following capability, while current driving VLAs themselves lack reliable instruction following under matched counterfactual tests.
2610.16634.title: Language2Drive: Do Vision-Language-Action Models Really Follow the Instructions in Autonomous Driving?

2610.16645.summary: Recovering divergence-free velocity fields from sparse and corrupted observations requires reconciling physical consistency, expressive representations, and robustness to missing data. We introduce DFK-Former, a set-to-field transformer that reconstructs divergence-free velocity fields from sparse, noisy, and irregularly sampled 3D observations. The model is inherently invariant to the number and ordering of input samples and predicts the parameters of a divergence-free kernel representation, producing continuous, mesh-free velocity fields that satisfy incompressibility exactly by construction rather than approximately through soft constraints or projection operators. Unlike existing divergence-free kernel approaches, which estimate kernel coefficients via a separate optimization for each field, DFK-Former predicts these coefficients directly in a single forward pass. This eliminates costly iterative fitting while providing a learned prior that enables accurate reconstruction even when observations are insufficient to uniquely determine the field. To enhance representational power, we introduce adaptive and anisotropic divergence-free kernels that preserve exact incompressibility guarantees while capturing more complex flow structures. Extensive experiments across varying levels of sparsity, noise, and occlusion, including transfer to real Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) turbulence data, demonstrate substantial gains in both accuracy and efficiency. DFK-Former reduces endpoint error by up to 4.6x compared to per-field divergence-free-kernel optimization, while reconstructing each field in 7.5 ms instead of 9.8 s, yielding a speedup of more than three orders of magnitude. These results establish direct, feed-forward prediction of divergence-free kernel parameters as a practical and effective paradigm for physically consistent velocity-field reconstruction from sparse observations.
2610.16645.title: Learning Incompressible 3D Flows from Sparse Samples: A Set Transformer Approach to Divergence-Free Kernel Fitting

2610.16649.summary: The sums of the absolute values of higher-order cumulants are classical contrast functions for independent component analysis (ICA) and lead naturally to robust approximate diagonalization of higher-order cumulant tensors using $\ell_1$-based diagonalization over the orthogonal or unitary group. We propose Jacobi-SubG, a Jacobi-type framework that selects index pairs using Riemannian subdifferential information and performs plane rotations with a refinement step that preserves nonzero diagonal contractions. For the general tensor model, we prove global convergence of the entire iterate sequence from any initialization with nonzero diagonal contractions, provided that the subproblem solvers satisfy a uniform sufficient-ascent estimate. For real and complex third- and fourth-order cumulant tensors, which are widely used in ICA, we develop specialized subproblem solvers satisfying these conditions. The resulting algorithms thus enjoy global convergence under the simple initialization condition that all diagonal contractions are nonzero. Numerical experiments on ICA and tensor diagonalization show that the proposed Jacobi-SubG variants achieve better source recovery and higher final objective values in several settings, particularly at the higher tested noise levels.
2610.16649.title: Globally Convergent Jacobi-Type Algorithms for Robust Approximate Diagonalization of Higher-Order Cumulant Tensors

2610.16782.summary: Industrial manipulation in flexible manufacturing, e.g., high-mix, low-volume (HMLV) electronics assembly, requires robot policies to adapt to changing products and production conditions. Such settings impose industrial process constraints, including product variants, moving material flows, finite execution windows, and tight geometric tolerances. However, existing evaluation frameworks do not systematically capture these constraints when assessing generalist robot policies. To address this gap, we introduce LIBERO-Industry, a novel benchmark built on the widely used robot learning benchmark LIBERO, that translates the aforementioned industrial constraints into controllable task conditions and measurable success criteria. Specifically, LIBERO-Industry comprises three classic task scenarios: Static-to-Dynamic (S2D) loading, Dynamic-to-Static (D2S) unloading, and Dynamic-to-Dynamic (D2D) transfer. The suites contain 216 tasks in total that systematically vary object geometry, conveyor speed, interaction-window duration, and geometric acceptance region size. Extensive experiments across five generalist robot policies (including vision-language-action models and world-action models) show that performance progressively degrades as industrial constraints are introduced and combined. Under a shared fine-tuning and evaluation protocol, the LIBERO-Industry co-training condition achieved higher observed target-transfer completion than the original-LIBERO condition.
2610.16782.title: LIBERO-Industry: Benchmarking Robotic Manipulation under Industrial Process Constraints

2610.16814.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to assign scalar scores that drive downstream decision-making, including tasks such as paper review and recommendation. However, LLM-as-a-Judge pipelines are vulnerable to score-hijacking prompt injection embedded in evaluated content, which corrupts scoring signals and distorts induced rankings. Existing defenses often enforce robustness by modifying the judge model itself, making safety dependent on a specific model's scale and training and requiring repeated effort when the judge is updated or replaced. We propose StableJudge, a lightweight defense framework that externalizes prompt-injection mitigation as a reusable pre-scoring capability. StableJudge centers on a compact 0.13B Sentry that localizes injected spans and performs targeted sanitization prior to evaluation, and is trained using adversarially evolving attacks to improve robustness beyond a fixed prompt set. To stabilize measurement, StableJudge derives deterministic, fine-grained scalar scores from the judge's output distribution. Across held-out scientific abstracts and out-of-distribution attack variants, StableJudge improves score recovery under attack while largely preserving general-purpose performance, demonstrating that robust LLM-based judging can be achieved by decoupling safety from judge scale via reusable defense capabilities. Code and data will be released.
2610.16814.title: StableJudge: A Lightweight Adversarial Defense Framework for LLM-as-a-Judge

2610.16845.summary: Standardizing a rare feature can help stochastic gradient descent learn its effect within a finite budget, but it also changes the noise cost of learning. We characterize the lowest rare-subgroup risks attainable by standardized and unscaled training when each chooses a nonnegative constant learning rate and a deterministic stopping time under the same observation cap. For two independent binary features, we derive both optimized risks as prevalence vanishes while the expected number of rare observations remains finite. Uniform control over rates and stopping times reduces each limiting oracle to a scalar minimization. With positive noise, the preferred scaling changes exactly once as we move signal to the rare feature while the limiting risk at initialization stays fixed and positive. The formulas also explain how noise and budget affect the comparison. Separate finite-prevalence bounds favor standardization on a rare-dominant signal family and unscaled training on a common-dominant family. The results concern final iterates with population preprocessing and fresh observations. Exact-moment searches assess the approximation at finite prevalence. In a controlled study, both orderings persist under observation reuse, estimated preprocessing, and intercept fitting when tuning choices are fixed before evaluation. Selecting a predictor after observing training can reverse an ordering, even when selection uses exact population risk.
2610.16845.title: Feature Normalization under Finite Training Budgets

2610.16876.summary: Target-aware multimodal instruction selection requires useful examples and an appropriate balance of supervision. Sample-level rankings can overrepresent similar content without optimizing this balance; group-level methods face coarse units, predefined set-level validation signals, and costly or inaccurate mixture search. We propose CLIVO, a target-aware framework connecting fine-grained semantic allocation, automatically learned validation objectives, and differentiable mixture search. Specifically, semantic clusters provide independently adjustable shares at the hundred-cluster scale. Correlations between per-example merged-proxy losses and real probe performance identify target-relevant validation examples; learned nonnegative weights combine their losses into an objective. A single backward pass through the merged proxy supplies gradients for all shares, avoiding an additional mixture-response regression model. Selecting 100K instructions from an 8M pool, CLIVO attains 97.2% of the full-data four-target average score with only 1.25% of the data. It improves on the strongest evaluated selection baseline by 1.16 points using random within-cluster sampling; combining learned quotas with sample ranking increases this advantage to 1.55 points. Analyses show that finer units benefit most targets, short-trained experts preserve mixture responses, sample weighting retains useful validation information, and direct search consistently reduces the learned objective. CLIVO also supports interpretable allocation, modular selection, and reuse across targets and granularities.
2610.16876.title: CLIVO: Differentiable Cluster-Based Instruction Mixing with Learned Validation Objectives

2610.16895.summary: LLMs are used as high-level controllers for embodied agents, but it remains unclear whether they support collaborative reasoning, such as anticipating a collaborator's actions in real-time teamwork without dialogue. We ask if observing the partner's state, exchanging object knowledge, and predicting the partner's next action, shape task outcomes and coordination when agents can share percepts but never intentions, plans, or task-level messages, and whether the two agents occupy symmetric roles. Using the Habitat-based PARTNR benchmark, we introduce a Decoupled Partial Observability regime that enforces strictly individual perception, and we augment decentralized zero-shot ReAct planners with Other Agent's State (OAS) observation, object Knowledge Exchange (KE) between co-located agents, and Other Agent's Next Action (OANA) prediction, evaluated on the full 2 x 2 x 2 grid with four planners on 1,000 validation tasks. OAS observation improves task quality, reducing extraneous effort for every planner, whereas KE primarily improves execution efficiency, cutting simulation steps by up to 25% with little change in success. The two are largely redundant for strong planners but complementary for the weakest, for which KE without the OAS is the worst configuration. OANA prediction lowers the success rate in 15 of 16 model x context pairs while raising explicit partner mentions to 55-100%, and its accuracy gains lie mainly in the coarse action type, partly because agents recognize the action the partner is already performing. The robot retrieves objects sooner and completes its tasks earlier than the simulated human. Shared context reduces total task time by shortening the remaining duration that the human works alone. Also, coordination benefits arise from responding to shared context, especially the OAS, rather than explicit anticipation, yielding shallow, planner-dependent partner modeling.
2610.16895.title: Observe, Share, or Predict? Disentangling Partner Information in Embodied Multi-Agent Collaboration

2610.16896.summary: We establish quantitative weak convergence for the joint terminal law of the solution to a stochastic wave equation and the normalized error of its exponential Euler approximation. For multiplicative trace-class noise and spatial regularity $α\in(1,2]$, the normalized error converges to its limiting distribution at rate $O(m^{-(α-1)})$, where $m$ is the number of time steps. This estimate identifies the leading weak bias and yields a first-order weak-error expansion with remainder $O(m^{-α})$. Moreover, by canceling the leading weak-error term, we construct a Richardson extrapolation scheme with weak convergence order $α$ for $α\in(1,2]$ and show that this rate is sharp. To overcome the lack of parabolic smoothing and control the remainders amplified by normalization, we combine dimension-uniform regularity estimates for the joint Kolmogorov equation with a conditional weak expansion and backward transport of coefficient directions.
2610.16896.title: Quantitative asymptotic error analysis and Richardson extrapolation for exponential Euler approximations of stochastic wave equations

2610.16911.summary: Does providing additional context to automated AI auditors improve their effectiveness? Using the Petri tool to audit LLM coding agents, we test the impact of providing two types of resources (an external codebase and benchmark transcripts) to LLM auditors, across four auditor-target LLM pairs and three behaviours (harmful compliance, reward hacking, sycophancy). (1) External codebase: We provide the auditor LLM with a fixed, external open source codebase, which prior work finds improves the realism of synthetic audits. Providing this resource suppresses reward hacking in both auditor-target pairs whose baseline rate is above the floor (4.8 to 1.3 and 3.9 to 1.8 on Petri's default 1-10 scale); the remaining two pairs sit at the floor throughout. The suppression recurs in three of four pairs under a different scenario and resource bundle. (2) External benchmark transcripts: We provide the auditor with transcripts of the target's performance on benchmarks measuring similar behaviours, intended to inform the auditor about the target's behavioural patterns. Providing this resource raises reward hacking scores in all four pairs (from 1.7 to 6.1 in one case). However, subsequent experiments show that supplying only the related benchmark's abstract, without transcripts, also increases reward hacking, and the effect is absent under a different framing of the same behaviour. Overall, we find no consistent effect of either resource outside reward hacking, but we find substantial variability in judge-scored behaviour across conditions. Our results underscore the importance of careful piloting with tools such as Petri, as the measured rate of target behaviour is highly sensitive to configuration decisions. We hope our results inspire more research into the reliability and robustness of automated alignment auditing.
2610.16911.title: Audit tools of the trade: Automated Auditor Elicitation Can Be Sensitive to the Context the Auditor Is Given

2610.16912.summary: An unknown ground excitation is recovered from the measured response of a rigid body sliding in two dimensions on an inclined surface under Coulomb friction, a system with no classical solution, whose sampled trajectories come from a time stepper. The Moreau stepper is shown to admit an exact inverse, explicit, non-iterative and vectorizable, giving the ground acceleration over each step in closed form, without regularization or an assumed source model. The inverse evaluates the friction direction at the end of the step, not its beginning. Inverting the continuous equation instead is not a secondary discretization choice: the two inverses differ by an exact identity proportional to the rotation of the sliding direction within the step, bounded by twice the frictional deceleration, which is of order one g for typical interfaces. The identity is inactive in one dimension, which explains why the sliding block literature has not confronted it. Verification against a manufactured reference solution recovers it to machine precision. On the field record, the discrepancy reaches 0.10g in root mean square, which exceeds the whole propagated uncertainty of the reported peak, and it suppresses 17% of the recovered travel, behaving as a bias, not noise, so root-mean-square agreement in acceleration understates it. The method is applied to surveillance video of a delineator post that slid in the 24 June 2026 La Guaira earthquake, yielding a peak ground acceleration of 0.912 +/- 0.047g, and a lower bound of 0.47g independent of the imagery. Displaced rigid bodies can therefore provide quantitative ground-motion information where instruments are absent.
2610.16912.title: Rigid Bodies as Accidental Seismoscopes: Exact Time Stepper Inversion and an Estimate of Ground Acceleration in the 2026 La Guaira Earthquake

2610.16920.summary: Antibody therapeutics have transformed treatment across diverse therapeutic areas and have become central to modern medicine. While recent machine learning approaches aim to accelerate antibody discovery through structure-based design and target-affinity optimization, successful candidates must also satisfy broad developability constraints, including structural compatibility, low immunogenicity, and favorable biophysical properties, while remaining sufficiently diverse to provide sufficient coverage of design space to mitigate later-stage development failures. We introduce a preference-conditioned multi-objective generative flow network (GFN) fine-tuning pipeline for fixed-framework CDRH3 loop redesign that fine-tunes a biological sequence model against many inexpensive proxies covering backbone compatibility, sequence likelihood, immunogenicity risk, novelty, and developability liabilities. It combines up to fourteen predictive rewards in a single policy trained to sample CDRH3 loops across 623 SAbDab antibody structures, leveraging a reward reduction strategy to preserve Pareto dominance under this learned map. We also introduce a novel autoregressive span-in-filling variant of AMPLIFY-350M that serves both as a scaffold-conditioned CDRH3 generation prior and as a direct conditional likelihood scorer. We evaluated reward scores, diversity, and design quality on loops sampled on 45 held-out antibody complexes to assess structural consistency, confidence, aggregation propensity, stability, and antigen binding. Compared with the inverse-folding methods ProteinMPNN and ESM-IF, our approach produces roughly 10x more distinct acceptable candidates per design at 50% sequence identity, while holding 10% of the 14-objective Pareto front pooled across methods, trading per-sample quality for greater exploration of novel possible structures.
2610.16920.title: Multi-Objective Amortized CDRH3 Sequence Sampling Diversifies Promising Antibody Candidates

2610.16940.summary: Nearest neighbor search algorithms are widely used and have a long history, but we find that key implementation details are seldom reviewed in articles about them. These details can materially impact performance, and thus change the conclusions one makes about a given algorithm's superiority. In this article, we highlight these impacts by reviewing the Cover Tree as an example, producing RustKNN, a unified Rust implementation of three construction variants of the Cover Tree with three query modes. Our analysis reveals: (1) the optimal query strategy depends on $k$ and on the dataset (single-tree search is fastest at $k{=}1$ on three of our four largest datasets, while dual-tree search is fastest at $k{\ge}5$ on the three largest), and choosing the wrong query mode can cost up to a $7.5\times$ factor in runtime; (2) the cover tree base parameter, set to 2 in theory and 1.3 in practice, is not a safe default for dual-tree search: 1.3 is optimal on only one of seven datasets, and on covtype it is $1.6\times$ slower than the optimum; (3) among five micro-optimizations, only early-exit distance computation has a consistent effect, and that effect grows with dimension (none at $d{=}32$, $1.31\times$ at $d{=}54$, and $1.49\times$ at $d{=}784$); and (4) all-nearest-neighbor and held-out benchmarks yield different implementation rankings. All main timing tables report medians over 20 independent allocations with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. RustKNN is open source at https://github.com/CrowdStrike/RustKNN.
2610.16940.title: KNN Implementation Details Can Dramatically Change Performance: An Example from Cover Trees

2610.16998.summary: Deep search enables language agents to solve complex information-seeking tasks through iterative web exploration. However, developing robust open-source agents remains challenging for three reasons. First, opaque trajectory-construction pipelines make training data difficult to audit and reproduce. Second, context compression can create a substantial mismatch between training and inference. Third, agents may retrieve benchmark content from the open web during evaluation, contaminating the results and overstating their performance. To overcome these bottlenecks, we introduce Glasseek, a fully transparent deep search framework spanning the complete development lifecycle, releasing all data, model weights, training recipes, and code. Specifically, for data construction, we establish a verifiable trajectory curation pipeline that systematically generates high-quality exploration paths. For training, we propose Compaction-Managed GSPO (CM-GSPO), which uses the same policy for search and summarization while optimizing only execution sub-trajectories, enabling end-to-end search-policy training across context-compaction boundaries. For evaluation, we conduct the first systematic audit of test-set leakage in open-web agents and release a modular anti-leakage plugin that seamlessly integrates into existing evaluation harnesses. Under this rigorous evaluation protocol, our 9B agent outperforms frontier proprietary agents across almost all deep research benchmarks spanning diverse task types, and achieves the best overall performance among recent open-weight agents, setting a new state of the art at the 9B scale.
2610.16998.title: Glasseek: A Transparent Recipe for Training and Trustworthy Evaluation of DeepSearch Agents

2610.17018.summary: Standard procedure in machine learning is to randomly split train and test data, emulating IID draws from one underlying data distribution. In practice, models are trained on past data and deployed in the future, which may come from distinct distributions. In this paper, we find that web text is indeed highly non-stationary, as text distributions shift over time. We further observe that model performance changes continuously over time across diverse benchmarks. Consequently, future model performance is better predicted by measurements made on recent evaluation data, and is best predicted by time series forecasters applied to historic performance rather than by historic performance itself. Choosing which model to deploy based on forecasted accuracy enables more reliable selection of performant models, thus improving downstream accuracy in the regime practitioners care about: deployment. Taken together, our experiments suggest that time should be treated as a fundamental variable in LLM evaluation. We release our code and data.
2610.17018.title: LLM Evaluation is a Forecasting Problem

2610.17057.summary: Vision-based document retrieval has improved rapidly, but current evaluation settings still emphasize short documents and single relevant pages. This leaves an important gap between leaderboard performance and realistic long-document retrieval, where the evidence needed to answer a query may span multiple pages or even multiple documents. We present VL-DocIR, a page-level benchmark for evidence-complete visual long-document retrieval. VL-DocIR is built from 29,641 HTML-born documents rendered into 388,548 page images from Wikipedia, arXiv, PubMed, and SEC proxy statements. It contains 271,760 queries across 23 domains and six evidence structures, covering single-page, within-document multi-page, and cross-document evidence configurations. Evidence annotations are grounded to rendered pages and HTML element identifiers, and queries are filtered with a cleaning pipeline targeting clarity, correctness, closedness, and the absence of explicit layout references. We evaluate leading single-vector and multi-vector visual retrievers together with diagnostic retrieval settings such as document-context scoring, query splitting, reranking, and round-robin ensembles. The strongest evaluated configuration reaches 69.3 nDCGAll@10 and 80.6 RecallAll@10 under structure-balanced Macro evaluation, but source- and evidence-structure breakdowns show that cross-document retrieval remains substantially harder than single-page retrieval, and that document-context scoring is especially helpful for within-document multi-page queries. VL-DocIR exposes these failure modes and provides a more demanding target for visual long-document retrieval. The new dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://yufanchen96.github.io/VL-DocIR.
2610.17057.title: VL-DocIR: A Benchmark for Vision-Based Long Document Information Retrieval

2610.17062.summary: We propose a mitigation to reward hacking in reinforcement learning. Our setup involves a misspecified reward function that gives rise to unintended behavior, and a monitor used to detect unintended behavior. As with frontier AI systems, the monitor makes systematic errors. Consequently, using the monitor for data filtering or to apply a reward penalty fails to prevent the model from learning unintended behavior ("reward hacking"). To address this problem, we introduce GRAFT: Gradient Routing Adapter Fine Tuning. Rather than penalizing or filtering flagged samples during training, GRAFT constrains gradient updates on those samples to a sacrificial set of new parameters. This has two benefits: First, because the monitor is not part of the reward function, the model does not learn to hide misbehavior. Second, ablating the sacrificial parameters reduces or entirely stops the unintended behavior while maintaining improved performance on target tasks. We demonstrate these benefits in RL environments where reward penalties cause models to learn to reward hack in undetected ways, training models ranging from 135M to 8B parameters. Additionally, we show a similar effect at a larger scale by distilling frontier LLM trajectories containing reward hacking into Qwen3-32B, without teaching that model to reward hack. Overall, our work suggests GRAFT may be a promising approach for leveraging imperfect monitors during post-training in settings where true performance is difficult to evaluate.
2610.17062.title: Gradient Routing Localizes and Removes Unintended Behaviors in RL

2610.17072.summary: Secure multi-party computation (MPC) lets parties evaluate a function over private inputs without revealing them. In garbled-circuit (GC) protocols, prior optimization has largely treated the number of non-linear gates, especially AND gates, as a proxy for cryptographic cost, and has focused on minimizing multiplicative complexity. We identify an orthogonal source of savings: a gate need not be garbled when one party knows or can locally compute its inputs; that party can evaluate it outside the secure protocol, even when the gate is non-linear. We introduce ownership-aware optimization for GC-based MPC, which minimizes non-linear gates requiring joint evaluation rather than total non-linear gates. We formalize this objective in a cost model and implement a compiler-integrated, gate-level framework that restructures Boolean circuits to increase party-local computation while preserving secure-computation semantics. The method is automated and general-purpose, and composes with existing multiplicative-complexity optimization. Experiments show that it reduces jointly evaluated computation and improves end-to-end GC performance on circuits with party-local structure, revealing protocol-cost savings missed by conventional GC cost models.
2610.17072.title: Think Locally Before Computing Jointly: Efficient Secure Multi-Party Computation via Maximizing Local Processing
