We introduce NavAble, a large-scale dataset spanning 11 accessibility-critical object classes, combining 41K curated open-source images with 8K newly collected, densely annotated real-world images. To extend scale and diversity, we develop a synthetic data generation pipeline that renders high-fidelity 3D assets across 37 environments under diverse styles and viewpoints, yielding 452K frames with rich ground-truth annotations from 565 assets. The pipeline minimizes manual effort by combining automated web image crawling, VLM-based filtering, SAM 3D-based asset generation, and convenient camera trajectory configuration, enabling large-scale data generation at a diversity unattainable through manual collection. Experiments show that fine-tuning existing segmentation models on the NavAble Dataset achieves reliable accessibility-object segmentation (>80% mIoU on our held-out test set). We also demonstrate the effectiveness of synthetic data augmentation, which yields up to +3.5 mIoU over real-world-only fine-tuning. Beyond benchmark evaluation, validation on egocentric data from two mobility-assistive robots demonstrates improved perception reliability in real-world navigation scenarios. Together, NavAble establishes a scalable foundation for BLV navigation perception, directly addressing the data scarcity and embodiment gaps. The dataset and pipeline are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/NavAble/NeurIPS_2026_BLV.
2610.19330.title: NavAble: A Large-Scale Dataset and Synthetic Data Generation Pipeline for Blind Navigation

2610.19362.summary: Best-of-N sampling is a simple inference-time scaling strategy for large language models, yet its behavior under incomplete reward models remains poorly understood. We study Best-of-N as a competition between the extreme reward tails of correct and incorrect responses. This view shows that success depends not only on the probability of sampling a correct response, but also on whether correct responses dominate incorrect ones in the upper tail. Using extreme value theory, we characterize three asymptotic regimes: correct-tail-dominant, incorrect-tail-dominant, and critical explaining both monotonic gains and reward-hacking-induced degradation. We further derive finite-sample scaling laws for representative reward distributions, showing that, under Gaussian rewards, incorrect responses with sufficiently large variance can dominate selection even when their mean reward is lower. Unlike oracle selection, convergence with an incomplete selector can be polynomial rather than exponential. Finally, we propose a lightweight tail-tension criterion to estimate when additional sampling may become harmful. Experiments on synthetic data and real reward model scores are consistent with the theoretically predicted regimes, scaling laws, and diagnostic behavior, suggesting that tail competition provides a unified lens on Best-of-N sampling for verifiable problems.
2610.19362.title: Tail Competition Explains Scaling in Best-of-N Sampling for Verifiable Problems

2610.19384.summary: Multimodal agents increasingly rely on visual interfaces to perceive state and select actions, creating an attack surface not captured by text-only safety evaluations. We study Visual Semantic Hijacking, in which deceptive but semantically meaningful interface elements, such as forged system alerts, cause an agent to depart from its authorized task. We propose a trajectory-guided procedure that identifies candidate injection points and inserts reproducible visual payloads into the observation stream. Using this procedure, we construct MMA-SafetyBench, which contains 1,083 adversarial trajectories across web automation, desktop GUI control, mobile navigation, document understanding, and video processing. Across nine evaluated models, Attack Success Rate (ASR) reaches 87.96%, while Semantic Compromise Rate (SCR) reaches 98.09%. A 1--3--5 scoring scheme distinguishes target-matching outputs, semantic disruption without a target match, and successful preservation of the benign task. Controls covering all nine models and five domains show that attacks persist under neutral prompts. A safety-priority prompt lowers ASR without eliminating the failure mode.
2610.19384.title: MMA-SafetyBench: A Benchmark for Multimodal Agent Safety Evaluation

2610.19399.summary: Korean neologisms arise through diverse mechanisms, a demanding test of language models beyond lexical memorization. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce NeoTrace, an automated, rerunnable framework that collects and dates neologisms across genres. Its 4,271 entries support KoAGE, a cutoff-aware benchmark with three acquisition and two generation tasks---the latter, to our knowledge, the first to compare model coinages with attested neologisms under their original materials and community context. Across 21 models, lexical recall diverges from contextual inference: in a five-model temporal analysis, models define only 13-30% of cutoff-year words, yet can infer meaning from one usage. However, structural understanding remains limited: even correct definitions barely improve formation analysis of pre-cutoff neologisms. Given word-building materials, single models often follow human formation mechanisms, whereas multi-agent coinage favors abbreviation and depends on interaction framing. KoAGE thus separates what models know, learn from use, and coin.
2610.19399.title: KoAGE: Do Large Language Models Know, Learn, and Coin Korean Neologisms?

2610.19418.summary: Lyapunov exponents characterize the average rate at which nearby trajectories in phase space converge or diverge and therefore provide a useful criterion for dynamical stability. In this work, we develop a general framework for analyzing Lyapunov exponents in stationary spacetimes and extend previous studies beyond circular orbits. For a generic stationary spacetime described by $g_{μν}(r,θ)$, we show that the phase space relevant to linear perturbations is spanned by $(r,p_r,θ,p_θ)$ and the corresponding linear stability matrix has rank four. When the spacetime admits a rank-2 Killing tensor, the linear stability matrix can be reduced to a block-diagonal form, allowing the Lyapunov exponents to be obtained analytically. By imposing the appropriate constraint conditions, the formalism further yields the linear stability matrices and Lyapunov exponents for circular and spherical orbits. The validity of the method is illustrated by several representative examples, including the (inverted) harmonic oscillator, planar Kepler motion, and particle motion in Schwarzschild and Kerr spacetimes. These results provide a unified framework for investigating the stability properties of particle orbits in both classical and relativistic dynamical systems.
2610.19418.title: Linear stability matrix and Lyapunov exponents for stationary spacetime

2610.19432.summary: Comparing financial disclosures across languages requires identifying shared accounting concepts and recovering all numerical facts that express them. Existing benchmarks evaluate aspects of these capabilities, but provide limited insight into whether both succeed on the same multilingual evidence. In particular, it remains unclear whether language models can recognize these concepts across languages and exhaustively recover their corresponding numerical evidence from the same contexts. We introduce MULTIFINGROUND, a benchmark designed to investigate this recognition-grounding gap in multilingual financial reports. Constructed from FY2025 disclosures of 90 issuers in English, French, and Greek, MULTIFINGROUND aligns independently authored reports through a shared accounting taxonomy and provides traceable fact-level annotations. The benchmark evaluates financial fact identification, concept recognition, exhaustive fact selection, and concept discrimination without candidate labels. Across 15 evaluated models, eight API and open-weight reference models achieve 97.3-99.4\% concept recognition accuracy, yet miss at least one target fact in 26.6-41.9\% of correctly recognized groups. Further analyses reveal substantial variation in concept discrimination and limited gains from the evaluated finance-specialized models. Our findings demonstrate that strong concept recognition can coexist with incomplete evidence recovery, highlighting the importance of evaluating semantic recognition and evidence completeness together.
2610.19432.title: Recognition Is Not Grounding: Benchmarking Multilingual Financial Evidence Extraction

2610.19477.summary: We study factorized gradient descent (FGD) for overparameterized asymmetric matrix sensing with the balancing regularizer $\frac18\|L^\top L-R^\top R\|_F^2$. An exact indefinite lifting of the population objective decomposes the dynamics of FGD into positive, negative, and null spectral subspaces. The first two components have linear restoring terms, whereas the null component contracts only quadratically. For independent isotropic sub-Gaussian sensing matrices and independent centered sub-Gaussian noise with scale proxy $σ$, we prove the local bound \[ \|L_tR_t^\top-X^\star\|_2 \lesssim\max\left\{\frac{1}{ηt+1/σ_r}, κσ\sqrt{\frac{d_1+d_2}{n}}\right\}, \] under a sufficiently small initialization error, the number of linear measurements $n\gtrsimκ^2(d_1+d_2)\max\{k^2,σ^2/σ_r^2\}$, and step size $η\lesssimσ_1^{-1}$. Here $σ_1$ and $σ_r$ are the largest and smallest nonzero singular values of the target $X^\star\in \mathbb{R}^{d_1\times d_2}$ respectively, and $κ=σ_1/σ_r$. Furthermore, a population trajectory was constructed to have tight product error $Θ(1/t)$. These results provide a local rate characterization for ordinary gradient descent for overparameterized asymmetric matrix sensing with balancing regularizer.
2610.19477.title: Convergence Rates of Factorized Gradient Descent for Overparameterized Asymmetric Matrix Sensing with Balancing Regularization

2610.19479.summary: Sim-and-real co-training is an effective way to scale robot learning by augmenting limited real-world demonstrations with simulation data. However, existing approaches typically treat simulators as fixed data sources, relying on uniform generation, offline retrieval, or manual parameter alignment by domain experts. We formulate \textit{Active Generative Simulation}: optimizing a simulator's data-generation distribution to maximize downstream real-world performance. To solve this problem, we propose MetaGenSim, a meta-learning framework that trains an auxiliary rater network via meta-gradients to automatically discover high-utility data-generation distributions within a user-specified simulation parameter space, without manual parameter alignment. Across simulation and real-world manipulation tasks, MetaGenSim outperforms uniform generation and retrieval baselines, achieves a 150% relative improvement in real-world full-task success over uniform generation, and matches expert manual alignment. We further show that distributions curated with a lightweight proxy policy transfer to VLA fine-tuning, and that MetaGenSim can exploit partial alignment through atomic skill stitching and object-receptacle composition when exact sim-and-real task alignment is unavailable. Project website: https://meta-gensim.github.io
2610.19479.title: Active Generative Simulation: Meta-Learning What to Simulate for Sim-and-Real Policy Co-Training

2610.19481.summary: Wrist-worn inertial measurement units (IMUs) provide a common sensing modality for tasks ranging from activity and gesture recognition to pose estimation, inertial odometry and clinical motor assessment. Existing wearable benchmarks evaluate performance across multiple tasks, but leave open how supervision for one task affects transfer to others and whether these tasks benefit from a shared representation. We present IMU-Bench, a benchmark of ten tasks from eight datasets for studying IMU multi-task performance and cross-task transfer. We compare six self-supervised methods pretrained on unlabeled recorded and simulated wrist motion, evaluating classification, pose and velocity estimation, and IMU-language retrieval. We find that our masked autoencoder, InrtlWrist, achieves the best or joint-best frozen-probe performance on nine of ten tasks, and fine-tuning improves on training from scratch on nine of ten tasks, including full-body pose, odometry and retrieval. Across transfer and joint-training experiments, supervision that benefits one target can reduce performance on others, with supervised sources transferring within kinematic estimation while, under frozen probing, none approaches the pretrained encoder on language retrieval, and joint-training gains that come at a cost to the paired task. These findings distinguish broad downstream usefulness from complementary task supervision. Code, task cards and a leaderboard are publicly available.
2610.19481.title: IMU-Bench: Benchmarking Wrist IMU Representations Across Kinematic, Semantic and Clinical Tasks

2610.19525.summary: Verifiable instruction-following benchmarks emphasize output-constraint satisfaction but can overlook whether responses meaningfully answer the underlying request, creating an evaluation blind spot. We show that frontier models can receive full credit for responses with little substantive answer content. Using the same verifier-based criterion as a training reward can induce reward hacking, as publicly released checkpoints exhibit higher constraint satisfaction but lower response quality after reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. To address this reward hacking, we introduce CALIF, a lightweight method that augments verifier rewards with a calibrated likelihood-based bonus to preserve response quality. CALIF evaluates response likelihood under the request alone using the existing frozen reference policy, requiring no additional judge or learned reward model. Across models ranging from 1.7B to 8B in reasoning and non-reasoning modes, CALIF improves constraint satisfaction on IFBench while maintaining response quality near or above pre-RL levels. It also outperforms corresponding base policies in 40 of 45 model-metric comparisons across three rubric-based instruction-following benchmarks, demonstrating gains beyond training verifiers.
2610.19525.title: Diagnosing and Correcting Reward Hacking in Verifiable Instruction Following

2610.19526.summary: Temporal action detection in long untrimmed videos suffers from inaccurate localization and low-quality proposals, especially with sparse annotations and ambiguous boundaries. For open-ended video understanding and LLM-driven event analysis, reliable proposals connect temporal localization, event annotation, and semantic understanding. However, conventional temporal action detection (TAD) pipelines lack explicit modeling of proposal localization quality, cross-representation support, and inter-proposal relations. We propose Hybrid Rank-Calibration of Action Proposals (HyrCap), a proposal-centric query-based TAD framework for temporal event understanding. Hybrid combines complementary video features with different localization cues, while Rank-Calibration adjusts proposal ranking confidence to reflect localization reliability and candidate competition. HyrCap treats dense query-based predictions as an over-complete temporal event hypothesis space. Cross-Representation Consensus Calibration, Localization Quality Estimation, and Proposal Redundancy Suppression improve proposal ranking reliability, localization quality, and candidate discrimination. Inspired by LLMs' capabilities in fine-grained semantic recognition, event description, and reasoning, we introduce HyrCap for Semantic Action Understanding, using calibrated proposals for standard TAD and as inputs to LLM-based semantic understanding. We define a staged evaluation protocol to separately measure event localization, segment-level semantic understanding, and combined event understanding performance. Experiments on public benchmarks show that HyrCap achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics and provides a finer-grained paradigm and evaluation protocol for query-based event segmentation and annotation.
2610.19526.title: HyrCap: Hybrid Rank-Calibration of Action Proposals for Temporal Event Understanding

2610.19568.summary: Latent reasoning replaces natural-language chains of thought with compact continuous "soft-token" representations, reducing the number of intermediate tokens that must be decoded autoregressively. We use a small external encoder to induce latent reasoning in a frozen backbone model. The encoder iteratively maps the backbone's hidden states to new latent blocks, constructing a latent reasoning prefix, after which the frozen model writes its remaining reasoning and its answer as text. Our method, INTACT, trains this encoder through distillation to reproduce the effect of written reasoning steps while keeping the model's behavior close to that of the frozen backbone, and then reinforces it on answer correctness. Across four frozen backbones from 1B to 8B, INTACT improves both GSM8K and average out-of-domain accuracy, including GSM8K gains from 75.8% to 79.3% on Llama-3.2-3B and from 77.6% to 79.7% on Qwen2.5-3B. It also reduces end-to-end latency per problem by 19% on Llama-3.2-3B and outperforms the evaluated latent-reasoning baselines at the 3B and 8B scales. Beyond the mathematics setting, the same recipe trained on a multi-domain corpus improves the frozen backbone on twelve evaluation benchmarks spanning mathematics, science, and commonsense, without task-specific adaptation.
2610.19568.title: INTACT: Inducing Latent Reasoning on a Frozen Backbone

2610.19571.summary: Real-world engineering drawings are often large-format and information-dense. Answering practical engineering questions therefore requires both fine-grained understanding of engineering information and complex reasoning over objects, relations, and evidence distributed across different regions or views. Existing benchmarks cover a range of engineering-drawing understanding tasks involving local regions, individual views, specific elements, or more constrained visual settings. However, systematic evaluation of understanding over realistic, large-format engineering drawings remains limited. To address this gap, we introduce LED-BENCH, a multidisciplinary benchmark designed to evaluate fine-grained understanding and complex reasoning over large-format engineering drawings, spanning the mechanical, architectural, and transportation domains. Extensive evaluation of 11 representative multimodal large language models, including 8 proprietary models and 3 open-source models, reveals substantial remaining difficulty: GPT-5.6 Sol achieves 52.65% average accuracy, performance varies across engineering domains, and all evaluated models perform worse on questions requiring broader evidence integration. These results highlight fine-grained understanding, evidence integration, and complex reasoning over large-format engineering drawings as persistent challenges for current multimodal models.
2610.19571.title: LED-BENCH: A Benchmark for Large-format Engineering Drawing Understanding

2610.19583.summary: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate text, their misuse has become a growing societal problem, with implications for academic misconduct, model distillation, and cyberattacks. For these reasons, Model Authorship Attribution (MAA), which identifies the source model of a given text, is important for promoting the responsible use of LLMs and improving AI safety. In practice, attribution systems must remain reliable beyond the distributions observed during training. They may encounter texts from unseen domains and writing settings, as well as generations from future versions of model families that were not available when the system was trained. However, existing MAA methods often exhibit substantial performance degradation under such distribution shifts. To address this challenge, we propose Authorship Tracing via Likelihood-based Attribution of Sources (ATLAS), which formulates MAA through source-conditioned text modeling rather than direct source prediction. ATLAS learns how text from each source family is generated and attributes a given text by comparing its likelihood under each learned source condition. We aggregate this likelihood evidence at the token level with clipping so that no single token dominates the decision. We further introduce MAABench, a broad MAA benchmark for evaluating practical OOD settings such as domain and version. Our experiments show that ATLAS consistently outperforms existing baselines across MAABench and OpenTuringBench. In particular, when both the generation domain and the model version change on MAABench, ATLAS achieves 74.27% accuracy, 9.00pp higher than the strongest baseline. Beyond MAA, ATLAS can also help identify distillation source models by measuring which source model a target LLM most closely resembles. Our extended experiments show that ATLAS recovers the known teacher of every distilled model we evaluate.
2610.19583.title: Who's Behind the Text? Robust Model Authorship Attribution

2610.19587.summary: Social psychology has long described how people can be persuaded to interpret a harmful act as moral. Recent research suggests that Large Language Models (LLMs) echo aspects of human psychology, from cognitive biases to social conformity. This raises a question with direct safety implications: can LLMs be moralized to bypass safety guardrails? We answer this question with a multi-agent framework grounded in Moral Foundations Theory (MFT). Given a harmful request that is initially refused, our agents diagnose which moral foundation (MF) the prompt is violating, identify a justifiable foundation under which the same request appears virtuous, rewrite the prompt accordingly, and reinforce it with generated precedents of comparable moral reframing. We evaluate our framework on harmful prompts from three well-known jailbreak datasets across five open-source and proprietary models. Our analysis reveals that models are highly susceptible to moralization, exhibiting high single-trial jailbreak rates with success increasing further under repeated attempts. We also find that safety benchmarks are imbalanced in the MFs they violate, concentrating on foundations toward which models already exhibit biases.
2610.19587.title: Moral Combat: Exploiting Moral Foundations Theory to Jailbreak LLMs

2610.19589.summary: Repeated event forecasting requires extracting predictive signals from noisy evidence and evaluating their value across successive decisions. We introduce JockeyBench, a benchmark and evaluation protocol that studies this problem through historical Japanese horse racing. The protocol combines time-gated evidence, priced tools, paired frozen-program controls, and two workflows: executing an LLM-written predictor or acquiring evidence for a fresh per-race LLM forecast. Evaluation separates forecast quality, benchmark-specific net utility, and retrospective betting returns and risk under fixed decision rules. Across 28 model--scaffold configurations on 324 races, paired tests identify seven revision gains and two declines after multiple-testing correction. Yet every configuration has negative mean profit under capped-Kelly settlement. In a four-model comparison, the reusable-program workflow has higher mean betting profit and lower research fees, although both workflows lose on average. Further diagnostics reveal that mean probability bias reverses on selected bets and that profitable individual runs can depend on concentrated returns. These findings motivate evaluating predictive competence, adaptation, resource use, and decision value separately when assessing agents for repeated event forecasting.
2610.19589.title: JockeyBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Horse-Racing Decision-Making

2610.19613.summary: As machine unlearning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) rapidly advances, rigorous evaluation of its effectiveness becomes increasingly important. However, existing benchmarks largely inherit evaluation protocols from text-only unlearning and overlook the unique challenges of unlearning in multimodal settings. In this work, we identify three major pitfalls that may lead to misleading conclusions: the lack of heldout evaluation to distinguish genuine concept-wise forgetting from instance-wise overfitting, the reliance on synthetic, fine-tuned knowledge rather than real-world knowledge acquired during pre-training, and unfair method comparisons caused by applying the same training settings to different unlearning methods. To address these challenges, we introduce GEMMU (Generalizable Evaluation for Multimodal Machine Unlearning), a benchmark built on real-world knowledge and a principled evaluation protocol. Re-evaluating representative unlearning methods under GEMMU reveals substantial generalization gaps and challenges conclusions drawn from previous benchmarks. Our findings highlight the importance of rigorous evaluation for advancing multimodal machine unlearning and provide guidelines for future benchmark design.
2610.19613.title: Are We Really Measuring Forgetting? Pitfalls in Evaluating Machine Unlearning for Multimodal LLMs

2610.19623.summary: Single-image 3D reconstruction has advanced rapidly, yet standalone garments remain challenging due to thin-shell geometry, open boundaries, and layered structures. Existing datasets and evaluation protocols provide limited support for systematic evaluation in this setting. We introduce MagicGarment, a benchmark for single-image standalone 3D garment reconstruction with 1,518 professionally constructed assets across 17 composite garment types, aligned multimodal annotations, and a unified evaluation protocol. We further establish a garment-aware reference baseline by adapting a pretrained image-to-3D backbone at two levels: Grounded Semantic Refinement (GSR) provides garment-focused visual conditioning, while Flow-Time-Route LoRA (FTR-LoRA) adapts the frozen 3D generative backbone using flow-timestep, token-routing, and expert-load information. Experiments demonstrate MagicGarment's benchmark utility and the effectiveness of garment-aware adaptation. Project page: https://1019538157.github.io/MagicGarment/.
2610.19623.title: MagicGarment: Benchmarking Single-Image Standalone 3D Garment Reconstruction

2610.19639.summary: High-frequency and broadband line-of-sight multiple-input multiple-output (LoS-MIMO) is a key solution for massive space-to-Earth data downlinks. However, in low Earth orbit (LEO) scenarios, it faces spatial rank deficiency from time-frequency coupling correlation and clock deviations from distributed oscillators. This paper establishes a dynamic effective channel throughput (ECT) framework incorporating waterfall characteristics of forward error correction. A hardware-friendly OFDM-based transceiver architecture with subband-adaptive truncation and dynamic timing recovery to achieve robust spatial decoupling is proposed. Through rigorous closed-form derivations, the equivalent signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) under joint errors is quantified, and an optimal scheduling algorithm combining truncation with variable coding and modulation is proposed to maximize ECT. Simulations confirm that the design circumvents outages caused by spatial notches with low complexity, stably enhancing the potential average throughput of a single dual-polarized beam to over 100 Gbps, providing a reliable theoretical foundation and baseband solution for next-generation high-throughput satellites.
2610.19639.title: Hardware-friendly Baseband Design and Performance Analysis for LEO Broadband LoS-MIMO Systems

2610.19652.summary: Recent work has sought to transfer first-order nonconvex optimization guarantees to zeroth-order methods through gradient estimators, typically incurring a factor linear in $d$. \citet{kornowski2024} obtained an $\mathcal{O}(dδ^{-1}ε^{-3})$ oracle complexity for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization and asked whether its dependence on all three parameters is jointly optimal. Although the dimension dependence and the first-order dependence on $(δ,ε)$ are separately known to be unavoidable, a matching zeroth-order lower bound has remained open. We answer this question in the unrestricted full-space setting. For smooth stochastic nonconvex optimization, we establish a scalar-oracle lower bound of $Ω\!\left(dL_0^2\min\{ΔH,L_0^2\}/ε^4\right)$ assuming a smooth, globally lower-bounded population objective and a second-moment bound on sample Lipschitz constants. A smooth reduction then yields a lower bound for Goldstein stationarity, proving the joint minimax optimality of the dependence on $(d,δ,ε)$ under explicit high-dimensional and small-accuracy conditions. Crucially, our results allow algorithms to query arbitrary points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, adaptively select sample-function labels, reuse the same sampled function at any number of locations, and output points without spatial restrictions. Thus, unlike lower bounds based on bounded query regions or fresh evaluation noise, our guarantees apply to a fully adaptive, reusable-sample scalar oracle. We also establish a separate noiseless exact-value lower bound against randomized algorithms, and hence also against deterministic methods. Our proof combines a globally defined sequential nonconvex construction with an exact Gaussian scalar channel, multistage random-field estimates, and an antithetic finite-sample realization that preserves information hardness under adaptive reuse.
2610.19652.title: On Global Joint Lower Bounds in Zeroth-Order Nonconvex Optimization

2610.19670.summary: The unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) and its stochastic-gradient variant, SGLD, are workhorses of modern Bayesian machine learning, but can be fragile when faced with a target distribution possessing a non-Lipschitz drift. In such settings, the expected squared jump distance can grow rapidly, leading to numerical instability or the need for prohibitively small step-sizes. We propose the saturated unadjusted Langevin algorithm (SULA) that pairs a saturated gradient drift with a gradient-informed state-dependent diffusion, while preserving first-order consistency with the Langevin diffusion. The drift and diffusion terms are chosen to guarantee that the one-step squared update is independent of the gradient. Consequently, SULA is robust to the choice of step-size and preserves estimation and prediction quality. We provide sufficient conditions under which SULA with a step-size $h$ converges weakly to the Langevin diffusion at the standard $O(h)$ rate, the SULA chain is geometrically ergodic, and that the bias of its invariant measure relative to the target is $O(h)$. Further, we develop SG-SULA, a stochastic-gradient version of SULA that rescales the stochastic gradient using a Gaussian CDF correction under Gaussianity of the gradient noise. Numerical experiments on various examples demonstrate SULA's robustness to tuning and SG-SULA's improved predictive performance.
2610.19670.title: SULA: Robust Langevin Sampling via Drift-Diffusion Saturation

2610.19679.summary: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in completing complex tasks through multi-step reasoning and tool interactions. However, recent studies have revealed that LLM-based agents can exhibit unfaithful behaviors, where their final reports fail to faithfully reflect their actual execution trajectories. Specifically, when agents fail to accomplish tasks through the intended sources or procedures, they may resort to alternative sources or strategies while failing to disclose such deviations, leading users to incorrectly believe that the tasks have been completed according to the original requirements. We refer to this specific form of agent unfaithfulness as Agent Completion Unfaithfulness. Detecting and mitigating agent completion unfaithfulness is critical yet remains largely unexplored. In this work, we propose MCAIR, a runtime monitoring and correction framework that leverages internal representations of LLM-based agents. MCAIR uses multi-step internal representations as inputs to train a risk-aware probe, enabling online detection of potential completion unfaithfulness during execution. Furthermore, MCAIR introduces a risk-guided correction loop that prompts agents to review their execution history and mitigate potential inconsistencies between their execution trajectories and final reports. Additionally, we construct ACUD, a dataset for Agent Completion Unfaithfulness detection that provides step-level execution traces, step-level internal representations, and consistency annotations for training and evaluating runtime detection probes. Experiments demonstrate that MCAIR outperforms LLM-as-a-judge baselines, generalizes across prompts and tasks, and effectively reduces agent completion unfaithfulness.
2610.19679.title: MCAIR: Monitoring and Correcting Agent Unfaithfulness via Internal Representations

2610.19699.summary: Proof-of-Stake (PoS) systems offer a scalable and energy-efficient alternative to Proof-of-Work (PoW). The economic security of PoS relies critically on incentivizing broad and meaningful participation through well-cali\-brated staking reward mechanisms. We study Ethe\-reum's effective-balance rules as a mechanism-design problem in which the protocol chooses a reward coefficient, an activation threshold, and a maximum effective balance, and validators respond in the induced propor\-tional-allocation game. For fixed participating validators and identity counts, we establish a unique Nash equilibrium in validator-level total stakes. When validators can split or merge their visible identities, each candidate identity structure must be evaluated after the market re-clears. Restructuring incentives therefore depend on post-reset payoff comparisons that account for all validators' stake responses. For an illustrative simulation, we construct address-level budget proxies from Beacon Chain deposits and withdrawals, Lido staking flows, Etherscan balances, and calibrated synthetic agents. With illustrative cost coefficients, lowering the reserve price from 32 ETH to 30 ETH increases active identities by 5.922\% and total effective stake by 0.098\%.
2610.19699.title: Effective-Balance Design in Ethereum Proof-of-Stake

2610.19704.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly help users arrange appointments, plan journeys, and allocate limited resources. These tasks require models to satisfy constraints on time, cost, capacity, and order, or determine that no feasible solution exists. Bangla is the world's seventh most widely spoken language, and existing benchmarks cover many language and reasoning tasks. However, benchmarks for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla under explicit constraints remain lacking. We introduce BANGLAPLAN, a benchmark of 1,000 problems across ten task families grounded in everyday life and institutions in Bangladesh. It includes feasible and infeasible problems in four language registers: everyday, formal, colloquial, and Bangla--English mixed. Answers cover eight structured types, including schedules, routes, allocations, and ordered steps, in a common JSON format. We construct the benchmark through language-model-assisted drafting and independent human validation. We evaluate 11 open-weight and proprietary model configurations using exact match, separately reporting feasible-case accuracy, infeasibility detection, and format errors. We find a large performance gap: GPT-6.1 Sol achieves 98.7% accuracy and Qwen3.5-27B with thinking reaches 80.3%, while direct-answer configurations score at most 30.9%. Seven of eleven configurations perform below the always-``infeasible'' baseline. Our findings also suggest that harder problems primarily reduce plan-construction accuracy, while infeasibility detection remains more robust. BANGLAPLAN provides a reproducible basis for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla. BANGLAPLAN is available at: https://github.com/mrayhanulmasud/banglaplan.
2610.19704.title: BANGLAPLAN: A Benchmark for Constraint-Based Planning and Decision-Making in Bangla

2610.19774.summary: Zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) typically conditions on a short speech prompt, which conveys timbre but provides only limited evidence of a speaker's prosodic patterns. We formulate Long-Prompt Zero-Shot TTS, a task that uses long speech prompts at inference time to reproduce speaker-specific prosody without target-speaker fine-tuning. We introduce LP-TTS-Bench, a bilingual benchmark of 37 speakers with 63.95 prompt hours and 2,728 held-out test utterances. Beyond intelligibility and timbre similarity, LP-TTS-Bench evaluates timing, prominence, intonation, and model-based prosody metrics, enabling multidimensional evaluation of prosody reproduction. As a reference system, we develop LPTTS, whose hierarchical Long-Prompt Encoder compresses long speech prompts into a fixed number of continuous prosody vectors. Experiments show improvements in several prosodic dimensions over a short-prompt baseline, with overall gains as prompt duration increases up to approximately 10 minutes and saturation at longer durations.
2610.19774.title: Long-Prompt Zero-Shot TTS: Benchmarking Prosody Reproduction Beyond Voice Cloning

2610.19832.summary: Reward model overoptimization in RLHF is usually described as reward hacking. We recast it as rent-seeking: the policy, a firm, earns reward from a regulator, the proxy reward model, that true quality does not back. The lens turns overoptimization into measurable quantities, namely rent, a capture index and deadweight loss, and into testable predictions from the economics of regulation. In a fixed, version-controlled testbed with three model families, accuracy-matched proxy reward models and two gold reward models, RL turns 41% to 66% of its proxy gain into rent while gold reward plateaus. Rent follows each regulator's prices. Neither proxy verifies facts, but one pays for confident specifics and the other for displays of diligence, so RL policies learn to fabricate details about nonexistent entities (97% to 100% of probes) or to deflect factual questions (67% to 98%). Kinship between policy and regulator adds a fixed premium of about 0.1 standard deviations but gives the policy no extra leverage under optimization. At a fixed expected fine, frequent mild audits beat rare severe ones, and random audits are as efficient per audit as targeted ones. Bringing the bunching estimator of tax economics to RL training, we also find a first sign that policies learn to stay just below a targeted audit's threshold.
2610.19832.title: Rent-Seeking Language Models: Reward Models Set the Prices, Frequent Audits Curb the Rent

2610.19848.summary: We present OpenTWBench, an open evaluation suite for Taiwan-domain knowledge in large language models, built around two benchmarks. tw-exam-bench contains 255,854 four-option questions across 148 academic subjects, from fifteen years of Taiwan's national examinations published as open data by the Ministry of Examination; answer keys agree across 31,312 duplicated question groups at 99.91%, with all 27 disagreements accounted for. A reviewed second pass withdrew 2,180 items whose stems depend on a figure the text does not carry; all scores use the remaining 253,674. tw-formosa-bench contains 1,696 difficulty-curated questions about everyday and contemporary Taiwan - the Taiwan that licensing examinations never ask about - generated from a community-curated corpus under a discipline in which no model writes a ground truth, and curated against a frozen seven-model pool so that the pool scored at the passing margin (46.9-74.6%, median ~54%); a leave-one-out experiment shows the selection preserves model ranking (near-zero bias). Within six weeks the frontier had cleared that band: of 108 models now on the public board, 22 score above its ceiling, the best 91.6%. We also document how much of a score comes from the apparatus rather than the model. On identical questions, switching answer extraction from pattern matching to an explicit \boxed{} answer moves accuracy from 20.8% to 93.9%; a single placeholder character in a system prompt moved one model from last (58.2%) to first (83.9%) on the same benchmark; doubling the thinking budget from 8k to 16k tokens bought 0.2% while shuffling which questions failed; and a three-judge validation panel proved to be one judge in disguise, two members approving 92-99% of everything shown. We release all datasets, per-item difficulty data, curation manifests and a leaderboard at https://opentwbench.ai
2610.19848.title: OpenTWBench (Open Taiwan Benchmark): Taiwan-Domain Knowledge Evaluation for Large Language Models, and How the Measurement Apparatus Shapes the Score

2610.19912.summary: Reliable validation of machine learning models is a crucial step in designing robust and trustworthy systems. Yet validation relies on annotated test sets treated as ground truth, even though annotations can be noisy or ambiguous. In object detection, sources may disagree on object presence, box location, or class label. Standard agreement metrics usually binarize box overlap before computing a summary score, obscuring the degree and structure of disagreement between annotation sets. Here, we study an Optimal Transport (OT)-based metric for measuring agreement between object detection annotations. Instead of binarizing bounding box overlap, this metric assigns graded costs to matched and unmatched labeled boxes. Through theoretical analysis and experiments on real and synthetically perturbed annotations, we show that OT captures graded changes in agreement and distinguishes annotation pairs that thresholded metrics score identically. Our results suggest that OT provides a richer measure of annotation agreement in object detection, especially for domains with many small or ambiguous objects. Such agreement estimates can support more reliable validation when labels are noisy or conflicting.
2610.19912.title: Quantifying Annotation Agreement in Object Detection with Optimal Transport

2610.20032.summary: Contact-rich robotic insertion is challenging because uncertainty in alignment, friction, and contact conditions can lead to unsuccessful assembly, excessive contact forces, and jamming. Designing a reliable controller therefore requires balancing insertion performance, robustness, and recovery from unexpected contact. In this paper, we propose PSO+TR, a derivative-free optimization (DFO) method that combines the exploratory search of particle swarm optimization (PSO) with a trust-region (TR) procedure for local refinement to improve the search process when progress stagnates. We apply the method to derivative-free policy optimization of an interpretable robotic insertion controller, jointly tuning its motion, feedback, and recovery parameters while preserving its predefined control structure. The proposed approach is evaluated on 93 eligible benchmark problems from the bound-constrained programs (BCP) collection and a synthetic contact-rich planar insertion task under uncertain operating conditions. Three random seeds per benchmark problem yield 279 matched problem--seed instances per method. PSO+TR reaches the prescribed target on 228 of these instances (81.72\%), the highest observed target-attainment rate among the five compared methods, which also include PSO, randomized black-box optimization (VRBBO), matrix adaptation evolution strategy (MAES), and differential evolution (DE). Across eight robotic optimizer seeds, the deployed controller-selection pipeline achieves 97.78\% completion under development conditions and 58.00\% under withheld stress conditions, compared with 91.22\% and 31.12\%, respectively, for the fixed staged controller. The stress violation rate is reduced from 20.69\% to 2.19\%. These findings support combining global and local search for DFO and structured contact-rich controller tuning. The synthetic planar results require validation on physical robots.
2610.20032.title: A particle swarm optimization with a reduced-subspace trust-region safeguard for contact-rich controller tuning

2610.20038.summary: Historical code changes provide convenient task boundaries, but do not identify which production functions selected tests exercise or support composing validated behaviors beyond a single change. We present SWE-Nexus, a fully automated pipeline that constructs repository-level implementation tasks from test execution. Four construction agents select tests, adapt tracing and evaluation protocols to each repository, and generate behavioral specifications. For each selected test file, tracing records an observed execution footprint of production function bodies. A scope is retained only if all expected scoring points pass in the original repository and masking the traced bodies causes at least one failure or error. Compatible scopes are composed deterministically, with shared functions counted once and every constituent test file revalidated under the complete combined mask. The benchmark contains 600 tasks from 105 repositories across six programming languages, including 116 atomic and 484 composite tasks. We evaluate 12 models under three agent scaffolds. The best configuration resolves 37.8% of tasks in one attempt, and scope-weighted scoring measures partial recovery. SWE-Nexus enables task construction from validated behavior beyond individual historical changes.
2610.20038.title: SWE-Nexus: Automated Composition of Software Engineering Tasks from Test Execution

2610.20118.summary: Multi-agent path finding (MAPF) solvers are evaluated on the schedules they produce, not on how well those schedules can be executed. Specifically, continuous-time optimal solvers can achieve even lower cost than their discrete counterparts by scheduling agents with near-zero temporal/spatial separation, and by exploiting graphs with higher connectedness; however, such schedules may prove hard to execute under a realistic controller. We integrate AOC-CBS, an anytime-optimal continuous-time MAPF solver, into a fleet coordination framework in which each agent tracks its timed path using model predictive control, and we evaluate the resulting system on congested MovingAI benchmark instances with 21 to 40 agents. Without intervention, only a fraction of the instances complete execution. We then apply T-robustness by adding a time-margin, i.e., a minimum temporal gap between agents at shared locations, as well as spatial inflation of the agent footprint. Increasing either margin raises execution success, for a relatively small increase in the schedule's sum-of-costs; it also improves how closely agents adhere to the schedule: when tracking each agent's position throughout execution and comparing it against the position it should occupy according to the schedule, the mean discrepancy falls significantly as the margin increases. In general, the two margins have different effects; temporal margin decreases deviation, giving the controller room to stay on schedule. Spatial margin affects deviation less and instead increases the clearance between agents, so that the same deviation no longer leads to a blocking stall. They are nonetheless substitutes rather than complements: spatial inflation is almost free in schedule cost, but its effect on execution success is small and does not compound with a temporal margin already in place.
2610.20118.title: The Cost of Executability: Temporal Margins for Continuous-Time Multi-Agent Path Finding under Closed-Loop Control

2610.20125.summary: We study the route-set allocation problem between end nodes in capacity-constrained flow networks with transfer costs. We introduce an origin--destination (OD) bidding language, in which a participant bids for bounded conic combinations of inlet--outlet--quantity licences and the mechanism performs the routing through a network-flow optimising winner-determination problem. We then study payment rules for the OD mechanism. Under a restricted model with openly and uniformly priced sources and bidders who are indifferent to the source of the gas, the Vickrey--Clarke--Groves (VCG) payment is core-stable; the key structural fact is that in this regime some optimal aggregate flows never use a physical pipe in both directions, so the winner-determination problem reduces to a single-commodity network flow whose value is submodular in the set of active bidders. If source access is allowed to depend on the individual consumer -- a realistic feature, e.g. when gas deals are embedded in bilateral political bargaining -- the reduction fails and VCG payments may lie strictly outside the core. For this general model we propose a dual (nodal) pricing rule derived from the shadow prices of the flow-conservation constraints, and prove it is always core-stable, at the cost of dominant-strategy incentive compatibility. Illustrative examples accompany each result.
2610.20125.title: Auction-based allocation of routes in capacity-constrained networks

2610.20127.summary: Identification of optically active defects in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) remains challenging because different defect candidates can produce similar calculated photoluminescence (PL) lineshapes. Here, we demonstrate that force-constant embedding methodology can be extended to calculate high-resolution, vibrationally resolved PL lineshapes in the polar layered material hBN. Benchmarking against the carbon dimer defect, responsible for the 4.1 eV emission, we show that the methodology accurately reproduces the low-energy acoustic phonons and fine spectral features that are inaccessible when using direct supercell calculations. Applying the methodology to neutral carbon trimers ($\mathrm{C_2 C_B}$ and $\mathrm{C_2 C_N}$), we find that the calculated PL lineshape and excitation energy of $\mathrm{C_2 C_N}$ closely match the low-temperature spectrum of the emitter with a zero-phonon line at 1.54 eV. These results establish high-resolution phonon-sideband modeling as a powerful tool for discriminating among candidate defects in polar materials.
2610.20127.title: Identification of carbon-related color centers in hBN by high-resolution ab initio photoluminescence modeling

2610.20174.summary: Reinforcement Learning on Mixed-domain preference data (Mix-RL) has become the mainstream approach for training general-purpose Generative Reward Models (GRMs). However, Mix-RL suffers from two critical bottlenecks: the reward sparsity induced by outcome rewards, and the cross-domain interference arising from jointly optimizing heterogeneous capabilities, which together give rise to imbalanced capability acquisition and pervasive reward hacking. Inspired by the success of On-Policy Distillation (OPD) in multi-domain capability integration, we introduce RM-OPD (Reward Modeling via On-Policy Distillation), a two-stage framework that separates specialist acquisition from capability integration. First, we cultivate domain-specialized teacher models via single-domain GRPO fine-tuning, allowing each expert to reach its performance ceiling in isolation; then we consolidate these teachers into one student model through (i) routed on-policy distillation, which provides dense signed token-level supervision on student-generated critiques; (ii) domain contribution reweighting, which reweights token guidance toward target domain shares, preventing specific domains from dominating optimization; and (iii) optional criteria context distillation, which conditions teachers on domain-specific evaluation criteria to sharpen token-level supervision. Across multiple RM benchmarks and two base models, RM-OPD consistently outperforms vanilla Mix-RL and other strong baselines, achieving overall superior performance and exhibiting an emergent "teacher-surpassing" effect. These results establish RM-OPD as a promising paradigm for building generalist GRMs.
2610.20174.title: RM-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Generative Reward Models

2610.20219.summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) equips cellular networks with the dual capability of data transmission and environmental sensing by sharing spectrum, waveforms, and radio hardware. While network-side sensing via transmission-reception points (TRPs) has been widely investigated, the use of user equipment (UEs) as sensing receivers introduces additional bistatic viewpoints and can improve target observability. UE-assisted operation is nevertheless constrained by small UE apertures and by waveform processing, especially when data-bearing communication signals are reused for sensing. The present paper investigates theoretical limits and operating conditions for UE-assisted passive target positioning, with emphasis on hybrid operation that fuses TRP--TRP and TRP--UE measurements. A unified OFDM-based signal-and-noise model is developed to cover both positioning reference signals (PRS) and communication waveform reuse with modulation-dependent noise enhancement. Based on this model, closed-form Fisher-information expressions and Cramer-Rao lower bounds are derived for delay and angular parameters and are mapped to positioning error bounds (PEBs) for two estimator classes: time-angle positioning based on TDOA + DoA and delay-only 3D ellipsoid positioning based on excess-delay/TDOA measurements. Monte-Carlo simulations across reference SNR, subcarrier spacing and occupied bandwidth, modulation order, radar cross section (RCS), sensing mode, and positioning algorithm identify regimes where UE participation and hybrid sensing provide significant gains and quantify the associated estimator-to-bound trade-offs.
2610.20219.title: TRP-UE Bistatic Sensing for 6G Performance Analysis and Insights

2610.20421.summary: We study the parabolic Anderson model $\partial_t u=Δu+βu\,\dot W_α$ on an unbounded Ahlfors $d_h$-regular Dirichlet metric measure space whose heat kernel satisfies two-sided sub-Gaussian estimates with walk dimension $d_w$. The noise is white in time and, in space, either white ($α=0$) or colored through the Riesz kernel of $(-Δ)^{-2α}$, where $0\le 2α<d_h/d_w<1+2α$. No recurrence is assumed. We prove existence, uniqueness and Hölder regularity of the mild Skorohod solution for bounded initial conditions. For nonzero nonnegative bounded initial conditions, the solution is positive and its moment Lyapunov exponents exist for every real $p\ge1$, independently of the spatial point and the initial condition. For $p\ge2$, these exponents have order $p\,(β^2(p-1))^{d_w/((1+2α)d_w-d_h)}$, with upper and lower bounds matching up to constants.
2610.20421.title: Intermittency for the parabolic Anderson model on spaces with sub-Gaussian heat kernel estimates

2610.20548.summary: Understanding the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly important for applications involving human-AI interaction and multi-agent environments. Social intelligence comprises two aspects: cognitive intelligence, the ability to infer others' mental states, and behavioral intelligence, the ability to select appropriate social actions based on these inferences to achieve social goals. Persuasion provides a natural testbed in which both aspects are simultaneously at play, yet prior benchmarks typically evaluate them in isolation using synthetic scenarios. We introduce PerSo, a benchmark that evaluates both aspects on real-world persuasion dialogues from Reddit's ChangeMyView community, using an LLM-in-the-loop pipeline to construct the evaluation tasks, validated through human annotation. Our evaluation of diverse LLMs shows that performance generally scales with model size but varies across dimensions. The strongest LLM slightly surpasses the best observed human performance on the behavioral task, while the best human participant remains ahead on the cognitive task.
2610.20548.title: PerSo: Investigating Facets of LLMs' Social Intelligence in Real-World Persuasion Scenarios

2610.20552.summary: We present KinoGen, a framework that synthesizes customizable humanoid loco-manipulation references through kinematically grounded video generation. KinoGen conditions a pretrained video generator on calibrated renders of the target robot and object in a simulated task instance and recovers the reference by fitting the same models to the generated two-view video, so that the reference lies in the robot configuration space by construction without a human body proxy or retargeting. Body, hand, and object priors initialize the reconstruction, and direct optimization against cross-view evidence refines it. Since an edited keyframe is simply another rendered state, a user can prescribe a goal object pose, regenerate the video around the edited keyframe, and obtain a reference that satisfies the pose exactly. Across eight loco-manipulation tasks, KinoGen yields lower penetration and foot skating than video-based baselines and preserves over 90% of annotated contacts, and its customized references satisfy every prescribed target with substantially less penetration than direct interpolation. Tracking policies trained on the synthesized references are deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands. Project webpage: https://kinogen-humanoid.github.io/.
2610.20552.title: KinoGen: Customizable Humanoid Loco-Manipulation References via Kinematically Grounded Video Generation

2610.20596.summary: Consumer smart devices observe the same human motion from different body locations, yet existing inertial-localization benchmarks rarely provide synchronized heterogeneous wearables with device-specific motion ground truth. We present CoWear, a dataset and reference framework for collaborative inertial localization using a smartphone, smartwatch, and smart glasses. The dataset contains over 30 participants, over 300 walking sessions, and more than 30 hours and 100 km of aggregate device trajectories, with each device individually tracked by motion capture. To enable collaboration across distinct body motions, we train role-specific estimators to predict the displacement of a common reference device over synchronized temporal windows. Their predictions are transformed to the world frame using gyroscope integration and fused according to learned uncertainty. Experiments using phone, glasses, and watch as reference targets show that multi-device fusion consistently improves both displacement and trajectory rollout accuracy over individual-device estimation. CoWear provides a dataset and reproducible baseline for studying collaborative inertial localization across heterogeneous consumer wearables.
2610.20596.title: CoWear: Towards Collaborative Wearable Inertial Localization with Multiple Smart Devices

2610.20598.summary: Achieving general spatial intelligence requires a unified understanding of both static 3D and dynamic 4D. However, we find that existing models struggle to excel at both: 3D post-training can weaken dynamic understanding, while 4D-specialized models often lack strong static 3D reasoning. Our analysis reveals that this spatial--dynamic interference is highly non-uniform across parameter groups, with the balance between static and dynamic capabilities particularly sensitive to changes in late-layer MLPs. To address this interference, we propose DynThinker, a unified framework for jointly strengthening static and dynamic spatial reasoning. Decoupled Exponential Moving Average (D-EMA) applies configurable group-wise averaging to constrain drift in interference-sensitive pretrained parameters while preserving flexibility for capability enhancement. Spatial-Dynamic Fusion (SDF) complements D-EMA by selectively integrating spatial and temporal priors from a dynamic geometry encoder into intermediate VLM representations under semantic guidance. Across ten metrics spanning nine static 3D and dynamic 4D benchmarks, DynThinker achieves the highest average score among all evaluated models. Notably, DynThinker achieves 56.0 on ReVSI, 67.2 on DSR-Bench, and 51.2 and 40.1 under the sample-wise and group-wise evaluation protocols of DSI-Bench, respectively, setting new state-of-the-art results among the compared open-source models across all four evaluations within a unified model.
2610.20598.title: DynThinker: Unifying Static 3D and Dynamic 4D Spatial Reasoning

2610.20667.summary: Rapid advances in AI capabilities are causing benchmarks to saturate. Once several models approach perfect scores, a benchmark loses its power to differentiate between them, and with it its utility for informing AI safety cases and frontier policies. Yet benchmark items produce far more information than the scores we typically extract from them: a full transcript of how each model solved the task. We investigate whether these transcripts can be used to assess model capabilities even after benchmark scores have saturated. We simulate saturation retrospectively using historical benchmark and model releases, and test whether protocols that access only correctly solved transcripts from saturated benchmarks can predict capabilities measured on held-out, unsaturated items. We evaluate representative contemporary approaches for extracting information from model transcripts: pairwise judging, single-transcript absolute scoring, and predictions from deterministic transcript features or embeddings. We find that saturated transcripts retain capability information beyond benchmark accuracy. Amongst our evaluated protocols, pairwise judging performs best, reducing prediction error by 5.3 times compared to a baseline using only saturated benchmark scores. This capability-relevant information is distributed across transcript sections, but concentrated in specific channels of information such as reasoning and tool-calls. However, the predictive power of protocols does not always generalise across distribution shifts -- for example by underestimating the capabilities of the first reasoning models introduced in early 2025. Saturated benchmarks thus retain capability-predicting signal in their task transcripts, but extending the lifetime of existing benchmarks requires methods designed to extract these signals robustly.
2610.20667.title: Evaluating Model Capabilities After Benchmark Saturation

2610.20743.summary: Many modern learning problems require comparing probability distributions whose individual observations are themselves probability measures, naturally giving rise to meta-measures in $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(Ω))$. However, optimal transport distances on this space can be prohibitively expensive to evaluate. We introduce the vertical sliced Wasserstein ($\mathrm{VSW}$) distance, a scalable metric on $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(Ω))$. Rather than slicing along the transport geometry of $\mathcal{P}(Ω)$, $\mathrm{VSW}$ projects each inner measure using continuous test functions and compares the resulting one-dimensional distributions with one-dimensional Wasserstein distance. We prove that $\mathrm{VSW}$ is a valid metric on $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(Ω))$, metrizes weak convergence, and admits dimension-independent statistical convergence guarantees. Empirically, $\mathrm{VSW}$ provides high accuracy and efficiency compared with existing distances for meta-measures. We further derive a practical particle gradient for the empirical $\mathrm{VSW}_2^2$ objective and demonstrate its use for gradient-based transport of meta-measures. $\mathrm{VSW}$ provides a simple and scalable alternative for comparing and optimizing distributions of distributions.
2610.20743.title: Vertical Sliced Wasserstein Distances for Meta-Measures

2610.20780.summary: In LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS), a local mistake can propagate as other agents build on it, turning a correctable error into a failed task. Diagnosing completed runs or repeatedly re-executing them to search for corrections does not provide a learned policy for intervening while execution is still in progress. We present Agent Runtime Inspection and Amendment (ARIA), a framework for learning when and how to repair ongoing multi-agent executions. Our key intuition is to turn execution-verified repairs into reusable supervision, moving repair search into data construction and training so that a learned model can intervene at runtime without repeatedly testing alternatives. First, we collect over 24{,}000 successful and failed trajectories across four multi-agent frameworks, six benchmarks, and eight host models. From these trajectories, we construct the ARIA dataset, to our knowledge the first large-scale dataset pairing failed multi-agent trajectories with execution-verified repairs. It contains 3{,}953 verified repair pairs, each specifying what went wrong, where to intervene, and how execution should continue. Then, we develop the ARIA framework for MAS-agnostic runtime inspection and amendment, designed to integrate with any MAS that exposes execution trajectories and supports continuation replacement. Using verified repairs as training examples, we teach a compact model to recognize when intervention is needed and how to correct an ongoing run. The aim is to learn repair strategies that apply to related failures in new configurations, rather than merely reproduce individual corrections. Finally, the trained ARIA model demonstrates strong repair performance in both post-hoc and runtime settings, with generalization to unseen frameworks and host models. Our code is available at https://github.com/LabRAI/ARIA.
2610.20780.title: ARIA: Runtime Inspection and Amendment for Multi-Agent Systems

2610.20795.summary: Understanding why listeners enjoy music is difficult because the experience is subjective and changes as a piece unfolds. Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a non-invasive way to study neural responses during listening, yet earlier work has mostly treated music emotion as a categorical label or relied on black-box models. We formulate enjoyment prediction as a regression problem on the public MUSIN-G dataset, which contains 128-channel EEG from 20 listeners together with song-level enjoyment ratings. Six deep learning models were compared under a participant-wise protocol, in which 15 listeners were used for training and validation and 5 were held out for testing. DeepConvNet, CNN-LSTM and GNN-CNN reached the lowest mean absolute error (0.97 to 0.99 on the 1 to 5 scale), while the temporal convolutional network (TCN) had the highest Pearson correlation with the ratings (r = 0.21). Gradient-based and occlusion-based explanations, averaged over all held-out windows, identify the time segments within each two-second window that most influence the TCN predictions. The study provides a reproducible cross-listener benchmark for EEG-based enjoyment regression and shows how explainability analysis complements standard metrics.
2610.20795.title: EEG-Based Prediction of Music Enjoyment Using Deep Learning with Explainable Temporal Analysis

2610.20798.summary: We study Huber regression in a heteroscedastic linear model in the proportional regime $n/p \to δ\in (1, \infty)$. Our main result is an exact characterization of the asymptotic empirical distribution of the Huber estimator. This characterization is in terms of three scalar parameters which determine the first-order centre and the asymptotic variance of the Huber estimator. The result shows that with heteroscedastic noise, the first-order centre may contain an additional component along the variance index coefficient. We derive the displacement coefficients that determine this centre, as well as the exact asymptotic variance. The analysis uses the matrix approximate message passing (AMP) framework to jointly track the regression and variance index coefficients, extending the existing framework for homoscedastic M-estimators. We illustrate the implications of this characterization by constructing a test for centre displacement and examining its empirical size and power through simulations.
2610.20798.title: Precise Asymptotics for Dense High-Dimensional Huber Regression under Heteroscedasticity

2610.20810.summary: Readout errors in superconducting qubits include incorrect state assignment, bit flips within the computational subspace, and leakage to non-computational states. These errors require different mitigation strategies, yet conventional measurement fidelity and repeatability metrics do not resolve their individual contributions. Previous repeated-readout studies have shown that temporal correlations reveal additional information about readout errors. Here we introduce the Readout Error Decoder (RED), which converts repeated thresholded binary records into a channel-resolved error budget. Controlled error injections validate the channel-specific response of the decoder. We demonstrate RED on both fluxonium and transmon qubits and across distinct leakage-lifetime regimes. RED identifies the error channels limiting readout performance without requiring dedicated discrimination of non-computational states, providing a basis for targeted readout optimization across different qubit modalities.
2610.20810.title: Syndrome-Resolved Decoding of Qubit Readout Errors

2610.20816.summary: Radio-frequency jamming threatens cellular network operations in contested environments. The Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) architecture exposes per-User Equipment (UE) telemetry through the E2 interface, enabling Key Performance Indicator (KPI)-based jamming detection without proprietary hardware. However, operational deployment demands detection methods that generalize across heterogeneous networks. We propose a Statistical Ensemble Method (SEM) combining adaptive Median Absolute Deviation (MAD)-based baseline detection, count-based anomaly detection, and abrupt change detection through a weighted voting system. SEM operates in two modes: a cold-start mode requiring no labeled data for immediate deployment, and a supervised mode where parameters are refined offline via grid search as labeled data accumulates. We evaluate SEM against five machine learning (ML) classifiers and five deep learning (DL) sequence models using approximately 25 hours of testbed data comprising logs from eight heterogeneous 5G environments, employing both single-environment and multi-environment leave-one-out (LOO) validation. Our analysis indicates that under conditions not encountered during training (distribution shift), learning-based models tend to lose recall and miss jamming events, whereas SEM, even in cold-start mode, maintains detection capabilities at the cost of false alarms. Furthermore, SEM's parameter optimization can be mapped to O-RAN's Non-RT RIC as an rApp for continuous refinement, allowing operators to transition to learning-based alternatives once corpus coverage is sufficient.
2610.20816.title: O-RAN-Native Jamming Detection Under Network Heterogeneity

2610.20835.summary: Long-term wavefront stability will be critical for the upcoming Habitable Worlds Observatory which aims to directly image exo-Earths. Mechanical and thermal instabilities induce slow, high-order wavefront errors which can degrade the contrast and in turn, the scientific yield of the observatory. Dark zone maintenance (DZM) has been proposed as a high-order wavefront sensing and control strategy to maintain contrast despite wavefront error drifts. This approach uses an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) to estimate the electric field at each pixel in the dark zone of the science camera. However, relying on individual pixel information to estimate wavefront errors can discard information stored in the underlying wavefront. This is a fundamental limitation on the best achieved contrast compared to the model based theoretical bounds derived from photon noise. An alternative EKF can incorporate more holistic information by estimating the drifting wavefront modes present in the system. In this work we analyze the performance of this Modal EKF on the High-contrast Imager for Complex Aperture Telescopes (HiCAT) simulator at the Space Telescope Science Institute. A parameter scan is performed across key variables: deformable mirror (DM) drift, the direct photon rate at the telescope aperture governing the mean number of photons in the dark zone (DZ), and the dither magnitude used to provide phase diversity. While prior studies explored a range of dither magnitudes, this work introduces a covariance-based approach within the Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) framework to optimally determine the probe magnitude required. Results from the modal EKF demonstrate a 15-fold improvement in contrast relative to the single-pixel DZM experiments, reducing the gap to within a factor of 2-3 of the theoretical bounds.
2610.20835.title: Modal estimation of high-order wavefront drifts on coronagraphic testbeds for high-contrast direct imaging of exoplanets

2610.20845.summary: Skill-policy co-evolution, in which an agent's policy model and its skill bank improve each other during training, is a promising paradigm for self-improving agents. Current evaluations score the co-evolved policy on the final bank it trained with (the delivered bank). After deployment, however, skills may be rewritten, added or removed more frequently than the policy model is retrained, leaving the policy to operate on a drifted skill bank that neither the training objective nor existing evaluation protocols address. In this paper, we first establish, through theoretical and empirical analysis, that the fragility hidden by this blind spot is not incidental. The acceptance rule these methods share (cooperative acceptance) ties a policy's competence to the bank it co-evolved with, leaving it fragile once skills drift, regardless of the implementation; empirically, sensitivity to skill drift grows as co-evolution training proceeds. We therefore introduce the CO-evolution Drift Audit (CODA), a deployment-oriented evaluation protocol that simulates skill drift and, alongside success rate under worst-case drift, introduces two new metrics: a consistency rate under meaning-preserving edits and a resistance rate to corrupted skills. Across four co-evolution methods and five benchmarks (six settings), worst-case success is 5-13 points below the peak measured for each delivered pair, erasing 52-93% of the delivered bank's gain over the no-skill baseline. CODA thus reframes the target of co-evolution, from peak performance on the co-evolved bank to the ability to harness skills however they evolve, and provides a shared standard against which future methods can be audited.
2610.20845.title: Evolving Together, Failing Apart: The Skill-Policy Co-evolution Trap in Self-Improving Agents

2610.20851.summary: Understanding when neural networks learn interpretable representations is central to mechanistic interpretability. We study this through identifiability: when can supervised learning recover the true latent variables underlying the data? We introduce two data generating processes distinguished by their causal direction where either labels cause latents (generative) or latents cause labels (discriminative). When the representation has at least as many dimensions as the latent space, we prove that the optimal encoders are linear in the latents. Conversely, when dimensions are insufficient, identifiability generically fails and encoders become nonlinear. We then show that additional constraints yield recovery of individual latent variables, not just linear mixtures. In the generative setting, non-negative activations and energy efficiency force each neuron to encode exactly one latent, providing a precise account of selective grandmother cell-like responses. In the discriminative setting, when latents are sparse and the true measurement matrix satisfies the spark condition, the learned encoder inherits compressed sensing structure, enabling sparse dictionary learning to perfectly recover individual latents. This constitutes, to our knowledge, the first identifiability result for undercomplete nonlinear independent component analysis. Our framework unifies nonlinear ICA, compressed sensing, and neural network interpretability, delineating exactly when representations transition from nonlinear distortions to linear representations and, under additional constraints or steps, to clean, axis-aligned codes. Theoretical predictions are validated on synthetic benchmarks and on activations drawn from vision models, large language models, and macaque inferotemporal cortex.
2610.20851.title: Complete or Sparse: A Tale of Two Identifiabilities

2610.20860.summary: Nonstationarity and heterogeneous dynamics are common in financial and macroeconomic time series. Volatility alternates between calm and turbulent regimes, interest rates follow monetary-policy cycles, and major events trigger persistent structural shifts. We propose the Time-partitioning Gaussian Process Mixture Model (TPGPMM), a Bayesian nonparametric framework for regime identification and nonstationary prediction that infers such regimes and their within-regime dependence from data, without Markovian assumptions. It combines (i) an adaptive Pitman-Yor process prior on ordered compositions, mapped to block lengths with contiguity enforced by construction, and (ii) regime-specific Gaussian processes for temporal dependence, yielding a nonstationary predictive distribution. By inferring its discount parameter, the prior adapts to homogeneous and highly heterogeneous regime lengths. Unlike sequential or Markov-switching methods, it flags persistent structural shifts as change points rather than reacting to transient shocks. A split-merge Metropolis-within-Gibbs sampler with exact Gibbs updates of regime boundaries jointly learns change points and hyperparameters in batch, quantifying uncertainty over the partition and within-regime dynamics. With an RBF kernel and a fixed, data-informed noise level, TPGPMM produces a sparse, confident segmentation. On simulated data it recovers the true regimes, and on the CBOE Volatility Index and the 10-year US Treasury yield it identifies regimes aligned with documented market and monetary-policy events. For prediction, variants estimating the noise level fit better than change-point baselines and fit and forecast better than the main specification, at the cost of a less sparse or less event-aligned segmentation; with a regime mean, they fit better than a fitted stationary Gaussian process and have lower forecast RMSE except at the shortest horizons.
2610.20860.title: Time-partitioning Gaussian Process Mixture Model

2610.20902.summary: LLM coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex can drive penetration-testing tools, but they reason about an engagement as a flat list of findings in a context window. Attackers think in graphs: isolated low-severity exposures turn catastrophic once chained through credential capture, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This gap feeds a common belief that AI agents cannot truly chain exploitation; we argue this describes the flat context window, not the model. We present ChainGraph, a pattern that externalizes exploit-chain reasoning into a Neo4j property graph wired to an off-the-shelf agent via the Model Context Protocol, no bespoke harness. Findings, attack steps, credentials, assets, and tamper-evident evidence receipts are typed nodes with pre/post-condition edges; JSON/Markdown holds documentary memory while Neo4j holds reasoning memory.
